en: The Amarakośa, also known as the Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana, Section 2:
In the Amarakośa, the second section is the Bhūmyādikāṇḍa (Section on Earth and Other Subjects).
Subdivisions of the Sections.

(2.0.1) The groups [of categories] are here declared with their limbs and sub-limbs as consisting of the earth, cities, mountains, forests, medicinal herbs, wild animals, and so forth; (2.0.2) and as consisting of humans, Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras.
This is the Earth Group.
(2.1.3) Bhūḥ, bhūmi, acalā, anantā, rasā, viśvambharā, sthitā;
(2.1.4) dharā, dharitrī, dharaṇi, kṣoṇi, jyā, kāśyapī, kṣiti; (2.1.5) sarvaṃsahā, vasumatī, vasudhā, urvī, vasundharā.
(2.1.6) Gotrā, Ku, Pṛthivī, Pṛthvī, Kṣmā, Avanī, Medinī, Mahī;
(2.1.7) Vipulā, Gahvarī, Dhātrī, Gaurī, Ilā, Kumbhinī, Kṣamā; (2.1.8) Bhūtadhātrī, Ratnagarbhā, Jagatī, Sāgarāmbarā.

(2.1.9) *Mṛd* and *mṛttikā* mean clay; furthermore, *mṛtsā* and *mṛtsnā* also denote clay. (2.1.10) *Urvarā* refers to land rich in all kinds of crops; *ūṣaḥ* is alkaline soil. (2.1.11) *Ūṣavat* and *ūṣaraḥ* both refer to saline soil and may take either gender; *sthalaṃ* and *sthalī* denote dry ground.
(2.1.12) *marudhanvan* and *samāna* are synonyms; *khila* and *aprahata* refer to two types of level ground.
(2.1.13) Furthermore, *tri*, *jagatīloka*, *viṣṭapa*, *bhuvana*, and *jagat* [are synonyms for the world].
(2.1.14) This world is the land of Bhārata, which lies to the north of the boundary of the Śarāvatī river.
(2.1.15) The regions to the east and south are eastern; those to the north and west are northern.
(2.1.16) The borderlands are the lands of the Mlecchas, while the Middle Country is the central region.
(2.1.17) Āryāvarta is the land of merit, situated between the Vindhya and Himālaya mountains.
(2.1.18) *Nīvṛt*, *janapada*, *deśa*, and *viṣaya* denote a country; *upavartana* denotes the same.
(2.1.19) In three genders, from *goṣṭha* onwards, when there is an abundance of reeds (*naḍa*), the forms are *naḍvān* and also *naḍvala*.
(2.1.20) *Kumudvān* is used when there is an abundance of water-lilies (*kumuda*); *vetasvān* is used when there are many cane-reed trees (*vetasa*).

(2.1.21) *Śādvala* means a place green with young grass; *paṅkila*, however, refers to that which is full of mud. (2.1.22) *Anūpa* denotes a region abounding in water; likewise, *kaccha* is a masculine term for such a place. (2.1.23) *Śarkarā* is feminine; *śarkarila*, *śārkara*, and *śarkarāvati* denote a place abounding in gravel or pebbles.
(2.1.24) These two [types of land] should be understood as being located in a region abounding in sand.
(2.1.25) A region nourished by rice that has been brought to maturity by river water and rainwater is,
respectively, (2.1.26) called *nadīmātṛka* (river-nourished) and *devamātṛka* (rain-nourished).
(2.1.27) A country with an excellent king is called *rājanvān*; elsewhere it is *rājavān*.
(2.1.28) A cow-pen or a place for cattle is *goṣṭham* or *gosthānakam*; when it refers to a place formerly occupied by cattle, it is *gauṣṭhīnam*.
(2.1.29) The ground at the edge [of a field] is *parisaraḥ*; a bridge is *setuḥ*, which is feminine or masculine.
(2.1.30) *vāmalūra*, *nāku*, and *valmīka* are masculine and neuter [terms for an anthill].
(2.1.31) *ayana*, *vartman*, *mārga*, *adhvan*, *pathin*, *padavī*, and *sṛti*;
(2.1.32) *saraṇi*, *paddhati*, *padyā*, *vartanī*, and *ekapadī* [are synonyms for a path].
(2.1.33) *atipanthāḥ*, *supanthāḥ*, and *satpathaḥ* are used for a road that is honored.
(2.1.34) *vyadhvaḥ*, *duradhvaḥ*, *vipathaḥ*, *kadadhvā*, and *kāpathaḥ* are synonyms [for a bad road].
(2.1.35) *Apanthāḥ* and *apatham* are equivalent; *śṛṅgāṭaka* and *catuṣpatha* refer to a place where four roads meet.
(2.1.36) *Prāntara* is a long, desolate road; *kāntāra* is a difficult path through a wilderness.
(2.1.37) A *gavyūti* is two *krośas* (feminine); a *nalva* is four hundred *kiṣkus*.
(2.1.38) *Ghaṇṭāpatha* is a royal highway; it is also called *saṃsaraṇa*; and the gate leading out from a city is called *upaniṣkara*.

(2.1.39) *dyāvāpṛthivyau*, *rodasyau*, *dyāvābhūmī*, and *rodasī* [are synonyms for heaven and earth]. (2.1.40) *divaspṛthivyau*. A *gañjā* is a salt-mine; *rumā* is a salt-pit. Thus ends the section on the earth (*bhūmivarga*).
The Section on Cities (puravarga): (2.2.41) *pūḥ* is feminine; *purī* and *nagarī* are optional [feminine]; *pattana*, *puṭabhedana*.
Now begins the section on cities (*puravarga*).
(2.2.42) A *sthānīya* is a *nigama*, while any other city that is not a primary capital is a *pura*.
(2.2.43) That is a branch-city (*śākhānagara*); a *veśa* is the resort of courtesans.
(2.2.44) A *niṣadyā* is a marketplace (*āpaṇa*), while a *vipaṇi* is a street of merchandise.
(2.2.45) *rathyā*, *pratolī*, and *viśikhā* denote a carriage road; *caya* and *vapra* (in the masculine and neuter) denote a rampart.
(2.2.46) *prākāra*, *varaṇa*, and *sāla* denote a wall; *prācīna*, *prātanta*, and *vṛti* denote an enclosure.
(2.2.47) *bhitti* (feminine), *kuḍya*, and *eḍūka* denote a wall; that which has bones embedded within it is called *eḍūka*.
(2.2.48) *Gṛha*, *geha*, *udavasita*, *veśma*, *sadma*, and *niketana*;
(2.2.49) *niśānta*, *pastya*, *sadana*, *bhavana*, *agāra*, and *mandira*;
(2.2.50) *gṛhāḥ* (in the masculine plural), as well as *nikāyya*, *nilaya*, and *ālaya*.

(2.2.51) *Vāsaḥ*, *kuṭī*, and *śālā* denote a dwelling for two people; *sabhā* and *saṃjavanam* refer to an assembly hall. (2.2.52) A four-sided hall is called *catuḥśālam*; the leaf-hut of sages is called *parṇaśālā* or *uṭajaḥ* (the latter being masculine or neuter).
(2.2.53) *Caityam* and *āyatanam* are equivalent; *vājiśālā* and *mandurā* denote a stable.

(2.2.54) *Āveśanam* is a workshop for artisans; *prapā* is a water-shed. (2.2.55) *Maṭha* is a dwelling for students and the like; *gañjā*, however, is a tavern. (2.2.56) *Garbhāgāram* is a bedchamber; *ariṣṭam* is a lying-in chamber.
(2.2.57) *Kuṭṭima* is a paved floor; it is not feminine. *Candraśālā* is an upper chamber.

(2.2.58) *Vātāyana* and *gavākṣa* denote a window. *Maṇḍapa* is a pavilion or a shelter for people; it is not feminine. (2.2.59) A residence such as a *harmya* belongs to the wealthy, while a *prāsāda* belongs to gods and kings.
(2.2.60) A *saudha* is a royal palace; it is not feminine [in gender], and it is also called an *upakāryā* or *upakārikā*.

(2.2.61) The *svastika*, the *sarvatobhadra*, the *nandyāvarta*, and others as well— (2.2.62)—these are the various types of *vicchandaka* that constitute the classifications of the dwellings of lords.

(2.2.63) The women’s quarters of kings are called *stryagāra*, *antaḥpura*, and *avarodhana*. (2.2.64) They are also called *śuddhānta* and *avarodha*; furthermore, *aṭṭa* and *kṣauma* (the latter being neuter) denote a turret or watchtower.
(2.2.65) *Praghāṇa*, *praghaṇa*, and *alinda* refer to the porch or vestibule outside a door.
(2.2.66) *gṛhāvagrahaṇī* is the threshold; *aṅgaṇa*, *catvara*, and *ajira* are the courtyard.
(2.2.67) The wooden beam situated below is the *śilā*; the wood situated above is the *nāsā*.
(2.2.68) A concealed inner door is called *pracchannamantardvāra*; a side door is called *pakṣadvāra* or *pakṣaka*.
(2.2.69) *Valīka* is the edge of the roof-covering (*paṭala*), and *paṭala* means a roof.
(2.2.70) *Gopānasī*, however, refers to a *valabhī* (gable), specifically a curved beam used for covering. (2.2.71) *Viṭaṅka* is a term, masculine and neuter, for a pigeon-ledge (*kapotapālikā*).
(2.2.72) *Strī*, *dvār*, and *dvāram* denote a door; *pratīhāraḥ* is also used for a door. *Hitardiḥ* refers to a sacrificial altar (*vedikā*).

(2.2.73) *Toraṇaḥ* (not feminine) is an outer gate; *gopuram* is a city gate. (2.2.74) *Kūṭam* is the "elephant's claw" (*hastinakha*) at the city gate; that which is [so called] is in the masculine. Now, [the following terms] apply to all three genders.
(2.2.75) *Kapāṭa* and *arara* are synonyms for a door-panel; its bolt is called *argala*, which is not feminine.
(2.2.76) *Ārohaṇa* and *sopāna* mean a staircase; *niśreṇi* and *adhirohiṇī* refer to a ladder.
(2.2.77) *Saṃmārjanī* and *śodhanī* are brooms; likewise, *saṃkara* and *avakara* denote sweepings or rubbish.
(2.2.78) *Kṣipta* means thrown; *niḥsaraṇa*, *saṃniveśa*, and *nikarṣaṇa* mean exit or settlement.

(2.2.79) *Saṃvasatha* and *grāma* are synonyms; *veśma-bhū* and *vāstu* are feminine terms for the site of a dwelling. (2.2.80) *Upaśalya* refers to the outskirts of a village; both *sīmā* and *sīman* (the latter being feminine) denote a boundary.
(2.2.81) *Ghoṣa* is a cowherd settlement (*ābhīrapallī*); *pakkaṇa* is the abode of the Śabaras. Thus ends the section on cities; now follows the section on mountains.
(2.3.82) Mahīdhra, śikhari, kṣmābhṛt, ahārya, dhara, and parvata [are synonyms for mountain].
Now, the section on mountains (2.3.83): Adri, gotra, giri, grāvan, acala, śaila, and śiloccaya [are synonyms for mountain].

(2.3.84) Lokāloka is the Cakravāla; Trikuṭa and Trikūṭa are synonyms. (2.3.85) Asta is the western mountain; Udaya is the eastern mountain. (2.3.86) Himavat, Niṣadha, Vindhya, Mālyavat, and Pāriyātrika [are the principal mountain ranges].
(2.3.87) Gandhamādana and other mountains such as Hemakūṭa;
(2.3.88) pāṣāṇa, prastara, grāvan, upala, aśman, śilā, and dṛṣad denote stone;
(2.3.89) kūṭa, śikhara, and śṛṅga (which may be masculine or neuter) denote a peak, while prapāta, ataṭa, and bhṛgu denote a precipice.

(2.3.90) *kaṭaka* (masculine/neuter), *nitamba*, and *snu* denote the slope of a mountain; *prastha* and *sānu* (both neuter) denote the ridge. (2.3.91) *utsa*, *prasravaṇa*, *vāripravāha*, *nirjhara*, and *jhara* denote a spring or waterfall.
(2.3.92) *darī* (feminine) and *kandara* (masculine/feminine) denote a cave; *guhā* (feminine) denotes a cave dug by the gods or a natural cavern.
(2.3.93) *Gahvara* refers to a cave; *gaṇḍaśailāḥ* are large boulders fallen from a mountain.
(2.3.94) *Dantakāḥ* are the protruding ridges on the exterior of a mountain. (2.3.95) *Khaniḥ* (feminine) and *ākaraḥ* denote a mine; *pādāḥ* refers to the foothills or surrounding mountains.
(2.3.96) *Upatyakā* is the land at the base of a mountain; *adhityakā* is the land above it.
(2.3.97) *Dhātu* refers to minerals such as realgar (*manaḥśilā*) and especially red ochre (*gairika*) found on a mountain.
(2.3.98) *Nikuñja* and *kuñja* are used for a place covered by creepers and the like, and they may be neuter.
Thus ends the section on mountains;
now the section on forest flora.
(2.4.99) Aṭavī, araṇya, vipina, gahana, kānana, and vana all mean forest.

Now begins the section on forest herbs (2.4.100). A vast wilderness is called *araṇyānī*; whereas *niṣkuṭas* are garden groves near a house (2.4.101). An *ārāma* is a pleasure grove, which is simply a forest that has been artificially cultivated.
(2.4.102) A grove of trees in the garden of a minister’s house or a courtesan’s house is called a *vṛkṣavāṭikā*.

(2.4.103) A pleasure-garden for men belonging to a king is an *udyāna*, which is a common forest. (2.4.104) That very same [garden], when suitable for the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*), is called a *pramadavana*.

(2.4.105) *Vīthī*, *ālī*, *āvalī*, *paṅkti*, and *śreṇī* mean a row; *lekhā* and *rājayaḥ* mean lines or streaks. (2.4.106) *Vanyā* refers to a collection of forests; *aṅkura* is a new sprout or shoot.
(2.4.107) *Vṛkṣa*, *mahīruha*, *śākhī*, *viṭapī*, *pādapa*, and *taru* all denote a tree.
(2.4.108) *anokaha*, *kuṭa*, *śāla*, *palāśin*, *dru*, *druma*, and *agama* [are synonyms for tree].
(2.4.109) A *vānaspatya* is that which bears fruit from flowers; one that bears fruit without flowers is a *vanaspati*.
(2.4.110) Plants that perish at the ripening of their fruit are called *oṣadhi*; one that bears fruit is called *phalegrahi* (fruit-bearing).
(2.4.111) *vandhya* means "barren," while *aphala*, *avakeśin*, *phalavat*, *phalina*, and *phalī* mean "fruit-bearing.

(2.4.112) *praphulla*, *utphulla*, *saṃphulla*, *vyākośa*, *vikaca*, and *sphuṭa*— (2.4.113)—as well as *phulla*, these [terms] denote that which has blossomed; *avandhya* and the others apply to all three genders.
(2.4.114) A *sthāṇu* is a tree stump; a *nā* is a fixed peg; a *kṣupa* is a shrub with short branches and roots.
(2.4.115) When lacking a trunk (*aprakāṇḍa*), they are called *stamba* or *gulma*; a *vallī*, *vratati*, or *latā* is a creeper.
(2.4.116) A *latā* is a spreading creeper; a *vīrud* is a spreading plant, as are those called *gulminī* and *ulapa*.
(2.4.117) The ascent to a mountain and so forth is called *ucchraya*, *utsedha*, and *ucchrāya*.
(2.4.118) *Prakāṇḍa* and *skandha* are not feminine; they denote the trunk of a tree, extending from the root to the branches.
(2.4.119) *Śākhā* and *latā* are synonyms; *skandhaśākhā* and *śālā* are synonyms; likewise, *śiphā* and *jaṭā*.
(2.4.120) A creeper that climbs from the root to the top is called a *śākhā*, *śiphā*, or *avaroha*.
(2.4.121) The tip of a tree is called *śiraḥ*, *agram*, or *śikharam* (masculine/neuter); the root is *mūlam* or *budhnaḥ*; and the foot is termed *aṅghriḥ*.
(2.4.122) The pith or marrow is *sāraḥ* (masculine); the bark is *tvak* (feminine), *valkam*, or *valkalam* (neuter).
(2.4.123) *kāṣṭham*, *dāru*, and *indhanam* denote wood; *edhaḥ*, *idhmaḥ*, *medhaḥ*, and *samit* (the latter being feminine) denote fuel.

(2.4.124) *niṣkuhaḥ* and *koṭaram* denote a hollow in a tree (the former being masculine); *vallarī* and *mañjarī* (both feminine) denote a cluster of blossoms. (2.4.125) *patram*, *palāśam*, *chadanam*, *dalam*, *parṇam*, and *chadaḥ* (the last being masculine) denote a leaf.

(2.4.126) *Pallava* and *kisalaya* denote a sprout; they are not feminine. *Vistāra* and *viṭapa* denote a branch or spreading foliage; they are not feminine. (2.4.127) The fruit of trees and the like is called *sasya*; the stalk that binds the blossom is called *vṛnta*.
(2.4.128) An unripe fruit is *śalāṭu*; a dried one is *vāna*. Both terms apply to three genders.

(2.4.129) *kṣāraka* and *jālaka* are neuter; *kalikā* and *koraka* are masculine. (2.4.130) *gucchaka* and *stabaka* mean a cluster of blossoms; *kuḍmala* and *mukula* are masculine and neuter. (2.4.131) *sumanasaḥ*, *puṣpam*, *prasūnam*, *kusumam*, and *sumam* are feminine.
(2.4.132) *makaranda* is the nectar of flowers; *parāga* is the pollen of flowers (*sumanas*).
(2.4.133) All terms for the fruiting of plants are reduced by two syllables [in their neuter form]; *harītakī* and others are feminine when referring to the fruit.
(2.4.134) [The following are used] for the fruit: *āśvattha*, *vaiṇava*, *plākṣa*, *naiyagrodha*, and *aiṅgada*.
(2.4.135) The word *bārhata* [denotes] the fruit of the *jambū*; *jambū* is feminine, while *jambu* and *jāmbava* are neuter.
(2.4.136) Words such as *jātī* retain their own gender when denoting flowers; words such as *vrīhi* denote the grain itself, but [the same term] denotes the fruit.
(2.4.137) Words such as *vidārī*, however, denote the root as well; furthermore, *pāṭalā* is neuter when denoting a flower.

(2.4.138) *Bodhidruma*, *caladala*, *pippala*, and *kuñjarāśana* are synonyms for the *aśvattha*. (2.4.139) Furthermore, for the *kapittha* tree, there are the names *dadhittha*, *grāhī*, and *manmatha*.
(2.4.140) For that same tree, *dadhiphala*, *puṣpaphala*, and *dantaśaṭha* are also used.
(2.4.141) Udumbara is called jantuphala, yajñāṅga, and hemadugdhaka;
(2.4.142) Kovidāra is called camarika, kuddāla, and yugapatraka;
(2.4.143) Saptaparṇa is called viśālatvak, śārada, and viṣamacchada.
(2.4.144) For *āragvadha*, the names are *rājavṛkṣa*, *śampāka*, and *caturaṅgula*.
(2.4.145) For *ārevata*, the names are *vyādhighātaka*, *kṛtamāla*, and *suvarṇaka*.
(2.4.146) For *jambīra*, the names are *dantaśaṭha*, *jambha*, *jambhīra*, and *jambhala*.
(2.4.147) Varuṇa, Varaṇa, Setu, Tiktashāka, and Kumāraka;
(2.4.148) for the Puṃnāga tree: Puruṣa, Tuṅga, Kesara, and Devavallabha; (2.4.149) for the Pāribhadra: Nimbataru, Mandāra, and Pārijātaka.

(2.4.150) *tiniśa* is called *syandana*, *nemi*, and *rathadrura*; *atimuktaka* is called *vañjula* and *citrakṛt*. (2.4.151) Furthermore, there are two [names] for *pītanaka*: *pītanaka* and *kapītana*.
(2.4.152) For *āmrātaka*, [the names are *āmrātaka* and *kovidāra*]; for *madhūka*, however, [the names are] *guḍapuṣpa* and *madhudruma*.
(2.4.153) *vānaprastha* and *madhuṣṭhīla* [are synonyms for the wild jujube]; here, the water-born variety is called *madhūlaka*.
(2.4.154) *pīlu* is [called] *guḍaphala* and *sraṃsī*; however, when it grows on a mountain, it is [called] (2.4.155) *akṣoṭa* and *kandarāla*. As for *aṅkoṭa*, it is [called] *nikocaka*.
(2.4.156) *palāśa*, *kiṃśuka*, *parṇa*, and *vātapota* are synonyms for the *palāśa* tree; then, for the *vetasa* tree:
(2.4.157) *ratha*, *abhrapuṣpa*, *vidura*, *śīta*, *vānīra*, and *vañjula*;
(2.4.158) *parivyādha* and *vidula* are two [synonyms], as are *nādeyī* and *ambuvetasa*.
(2.4.159) *Śobhāñjana* is called *śigru*, *tīkṣṇagandha*, *kākṣīva*, and *mocaka*.
(2.4.160) When it is red, it is *madhuśigru*; *ariṣṭa* and *phenila* are synonyms.
(2.4.161) *Bilva* is also known as *śāṇḍilya*, *śailūṣa*, *mālūra*, and *śrīphala*.
(2.4.162) *plakṣa*, *jaṭī*, and *parkaṭī* are synonyms; *nyagrodha*, *bahupāt*, and *vaṭa* refer to the banyan tree.
(2.4.163) *gālava*, *śābara*, *lodhra*, *tirīṭa*, *tilva*, and *mārjana* are names for the *lodhra* tree.
(2.4.164) *āmra*, *cūta*, and *rasāla* denote the mango tree; *sahakāra* refers to that which is exceedingly fragrant.
(2.4.165) *kumbholūkhalaka* is neuter; *kauśika* is *guggulu*.
(2.4.166) *śelu* is *śleṣmātaka*; *śīta* is *uddāla*, also known as *bahuvāraka*. (2.4.167) *rājādana* is *priyāla*; *sannakadru* is *dhanuḥpaṭa*.

*Gambhārī*, *sarvatobhadrā*, *kāśmarī*, and *madhuparṇikā*; (2.4.169) *śrīparṇī* and *bhadraparṇī* are synonyms for *kāśmarya*. Furthermore, the two terms *karkandhūḥ*, *badarī*, and *koliḥ* refer to the *kola* fruit; *kuvala* and *phenila* [are also used]. (2.4.170)
(2.4.171) Sauvīra, badara, and ghoṇṭā; furthermore, svādukaṇṭaka (2.4.172), vikaṅkata, suvāvṛkṣa, granthila, and vyāghrapād;
(2.4.173) airāvata, nāgaraṅga, nādeyī, and bhūmijambukā.
(2.4.174) *tinduka*, *sphūrjaka*, and *kālaskandha* denote the *śitisāraka*.
(2.4.175) *kākendu*, *kulaka*, *kākatinduka*, and *kākapīluka* [are synonyms].
(2.4.176) *golīḍha*, *jhāṭala*, *ghaṇṭāpāṭali*, *mokṣa*, and *muṣkaka* [are synonyms].

(2.4.177) *tilaka*, *kṣuraka*, and *śrīmān* [are synonyms for the tree]; *picula* and *jhāvuka* are equivalent. (2.4.178) *śrīparṇikā*, *kumudikā*, *kumbhī*, *kaiṭarya*, and *kaṭphala* [are synonyms].
(2.4.179) *kramuka* is called *paṭṭikā*; it is also known as *paṭṭī* and *lākṣāprasādana*.
(2.4.180) *tūda*, *yūpa*, *kramuka*, *brahmaṇya*, and *brahmadāru*;
(2.4.181) *tūla* as well; *nīpa*, *priyaka*, and *kadamba* are synonyms for *haripriya*;
(2.4.182) *vīravṛkṣa*, *aruṣkara*, *agnimukhī*, and *bhallātakī* [are names of the marking nut tree]. These three [terms] apply in all three genders.
(2.4.183) *gardabhāṇḍa*, *kandarālaka*, *kapītana*, and *supārśvaka*;
(2.4.184) *plakṣa* and *tintiḍī*—the latter being *ciñcā* and *amlīkā*; then, in the case of *pītasāraka*:
(2.4.185) *sarja*, *āsana*, *bandhūkapuṣpa*, *priyaka*, and *jīvaka*.
(2.4.186) *Sāla*, however, is [known as] *sarja*, *kārśya*, *aśvakarṇaka*, and *sasyasaṃvara*.
(2.4.187) *Nadīsarja*, *vīrataru*, *indradru*, *kakubha*, and *arjuna* [are synonyms for the same tree].
(2.4.188) *Rājādana* and *phalādhyakṣa* [refer to the same tree]; furthermore, *kṣīrikā* [is used] for two [types].
(2.4.189) *iṅgudī* is the ascetic’s tree; *bhūrja* and *carmī* refer to those with soft bark.
(2.4.190) *Picchilā*, *pūraṇī*, *mocā*, and *sthirāyuḥ* are synonyms for the *śālmali* tree, which is of two kinds.
(2.4.191) *Picchā* refers to the fibrous covering of the *śālmali*; *rocana* and *kūṭaśālmali* are names for the thorny variety.
(2.4.192) *cirabilva*, *naktamāla*, and *karaja* are synonyms for the *karañja* tree.
(2.4.193) *Prakīrya*, *pūtikaraja*, *pūtika*, and *kalimāraka* are synonyms for the *pūtikarañja*.
(2.4.194) Varieties of *karañja* include the *ṣaḍgrantha*, *markaṭī*, and *aṅgāravallarī*.
(2.4.195) Rohī, rohitaka, plīhaśatru, and dāḍimapuṣpaka;
(2.4.196) gāyatrī, bālatanaya, khadira, and dantadhāvana; (2.4.197) arimeda and viṭkhadira [are synonyms for] khadira; kadara is [the name for] white khadira.
(2.4.198) Somavalka, as well as Vyāghrapuccha and Gandharvahastaka;
(2.4.199) Eraṇḍa and Urubūka, and that which is Rucaka and Citraka; (2.4.200) Cañcu, Pañcāṅgula, Maṇḍa, Vardhamāna, and Vyaḍambaka.
(2.4.201) A small *śamī* tree is called *śamīra*; the *śamī* has seeds like barley-meal and is auspicious (*śivā*).
(2.4.202) *Piṇḍītaka*, *marubaka*, *śvasana*, and *karahāṭaka* [are synonyms].
(2.4.203) *Śalya*, *madana*, *śakrapādapa*, and *pāribhadraka* [are synonyms for the same tree].
(2.4.204) Bhadradāru, drukilima, pītadāru, and dāru; (2.4.205) and pūtikāṣṭha—these seven are names for devadāru. Furthermore, [the following] two are [names] for two [plants]:
(2.4.206) pāṭali, pāṭalā, amoghā, kācasthālī, and phaleruhā.
(2.4.207) *kṛṣṇavṛntā* and *kuberākṣī* are synonyms for *śyāmā*, which is also called *mahilā*.
(2.4.208) *Latā*, *govandanī*, *gundrā*, *priyaṅgu*, *phalinī*, and *phalī* are synonyms;
(2.4.209) it is also known as *viṣvaksenā*, *gandhaphalī*, *kārambhā*, and *priyaka*.
(2.4.210) *maṇḍūkaparṇa*, *patrorṇa*, *naṭa*, *kaṭvaṅga*, and *ṭuṇṭuka*;
(2.4.211) *syonāka*, *śukanāsa*, *ṛkṣa*, *dīrghavṛnta*, and *kuṭannaṭa*; (2.4.212) *amṛtā* and *vayaḥsthā* [are feminine], while *bibhītaka* is of three genders.
(2.4.213) Nākṣa, tuṣa, karṣaphala, bhūtāvāsa, and kalidruma;
(2.4.214) Abhayā, avyathā, pathyā, kāyasthā, pūtanā, and amṛtā; (2.4.215) Karīrakī, haimavatī, cetakī, śreyasī, and śivā.
(2.4.216) *pītadru*, *sarala*, and *pūtikāṣṭha* are synonyms for the deodar pine; then *drumotpala* and *karṇikāra* refer to the *parivyādha*.
(2.4.217–218) *Lakuca*, *likuca*, and *ḍahu* denote the breadfruit tree (*Artocarpus lacucha*);
*panasa* denotes the jackfruit tree (*Artocarpus integrifolia*); *kaṇṭakiphala* refers to the thorny-fruit tree; *nicula*, *hijjala*, and *ambuja* denote the *vānīra* reed.

(2.4.219) *kākodumbarikā*, *phalgu*, *malayū*, and *jaghanephala*; (2.4.220) *ariṣṭa*, *sarvatobhadra*, *hiṅguniryāsa*, and *mālaka*; (2.4.221) *picumanda* is used for *nimba*, and then *picchilā*, *aguru*, and *śiṃśapā*.

(2.4.222) *Kapilā* refers to a cow with reddish-brown hair; *bhasmagarbhā* is another name for it. *Śirīṣa*, however, is *kapītana*. (2.4.223) *Bhaṇḍila* is also [a name for it]. Now, *cāmpeya*, *campaka*, and *hemapuṣpaka* refer to the same flower. (2.4.224) Its bud is called *gandhaphalī*; furthermore, *kesara* refers to its filaments.
(2.4.225) *bakula* and *vañjula* are synonyms; *aśoka*, *karakā*, and *dāḍima* are similar [in meaning].
(2.4.226) *cāmpeya*, *kesara*, *nāgakesara*, and *kāñcanāhvaya* are synonyms.
(2.4.227) *jayā*, *jayantī*, *tarkārī*, *nādeyī*, and *vaijayantikā* are synonyms.
(2.4.228) Śrīparṇa is agnimantha; kaṇikā is gaṇikārikā.
(2.4.229) Jaya, kuṭaja, śakra, vatsaka, and girimallikā [are synonyms]. (2.4.230) Kaliṅga, indrayava, and bhadrayava are the names for its fruit.

(2.4.231) *kṛṣṇa*, *pākaphala*, *āvigna*, and *suṣeṇa* are synonyms for the *karamardaka* tree. (2.4.232) *Kālaskandha*, *tamāla*, and *tāpiccha* refer to the same; furthermore, *sinduka*, (2.4.233) *sinduvāra*, *indrasurasa*, *nirguṇḍī*, and *indrāṇikā* are also names for it.

(2.4.234) Veṇī, garā, garī, devatāḍa, and also jīmūta; (2.4.235) śrīhastinī, however, is bhūruṇḍī; tṛṇaśūnya, on the other hand, is mallikā; (2.4.236) bhūpadī and śītabhīru are the same as that which grows in the forest, known as āsphoṭā.

(2.4.237) Śephālikā, however, is suvahā, nirguṇḍī, and nīlikā; (2.4.238) when white, it is śvetasurasā and bhūtaveśī; then māgadhī, (2.4.239) gaṇikā, and yūthikā are synonyms for ambaṣṭhā; that same plant, when yellow, is called hemapuṣpikā.
*Atimukta* is *puṇḍraka*; the *vāsantī* is the *mādhavī* creeper.
*Sumanā*, *mālatī*, *jāti*, *saptalā*, and *navamālikā* are synonyms for jasmine.
*Kunda* is the *mādhya*; *raktaka*, however, is *bandhūka* and *bandhujīvaka*.
(2.4.243) *Sahā* is *kumārī*; *taraṇi* and *amlāna* are synonyms for *mahāsahā*.
(2.4.244) Among these, when it is red it is called *kurabaka*, and when yellow it is *kurakaṇṭaka*.
(2.4.245) *Nīlī* and *jhiṇṭī* are two names for the *bāṇa* flower; it is also known as *dāsī* and *ārtagala*.

(2.4.246) *Saireyaka*, however, is *jhiṇṭī*; when it is reddish, it is *kurabaka*. (2.4.247) Yellow *jhiṇṭī* is *kuraṇṭaka*; in that [yellow variety], *sahacarī* applies to both [the plant and the flower].
(2.4.248) *Oṇḍrapuṣpa*, *japāpuṣpa*, and *vajrapuṣpa* refer to the flower of the sesame plant.
(2.4.249) *pratihāsa*, *śataprāsa*, *caṇḍāta*, and *hayamāraka*;
(2.4.250) both *karavīra* and *karīra* have the names *krakara* and *granthila*; (2.4.251) *unmatta*, *kitava*, *dhūrta*, and *dhattūra* are synonyms for the *kanaka* plant.
(2.4.252) *mātula* and *madana* refer to its fruit, which is called *mātulaputraka*.
(2.4.253) *phalapūra*, *bījapūra*, *rucaka*, and *mātuluṅga* refer to the citron.
(2.4.254) *samīraṇa*, *marubaka*, *prasthapuṣpa*, and *phaṇijjaka* [refer to the same plant].

(2.4.255) *Jambīra* is also [a name for citron]; furthermore, *parṇāsa*, *kaṭhiñjara*, and *kuṭheraka* [are synonyms]. (2.4.256) *Arjaka* is used for the white variety; *pāṭhī*, however, is *citraka*, known by the name *vahni*.
(2.4.257) *Arka*, *āhvā*, *vasuka*, *āsphoṭa*, *gaṇarūpa*, and *vikīraṇa* [are synonyms].
(2.4.258) *Mandāra*, *arkaparṇa*, *śukla*, *alarka*, and *pratāpasa* are synonyms here;
(2.4.259) *śivamallī*, *pāśupata*, *ekāṣṭhīla*, *buka*, and *vasu* [are synonyms]; (2.4.260) *vandā*, *vṛkṣādanī*, *vṛkṣaruhā*, and also *jīvantikā*.
(2.4.261) Vatsādanī, chinnaruhā, guḍūcī, tantrikā, amṛtā;
(2.4.262) jīvantikā, somavallī, viśalyā, and also madhuparṇī; (2.4.263) mūrvā, devī, madhurasā, moraṭā, tejanī, and sravā.
(2.4.264) Madhūlikā, madhuśreṇī, gokarṇī, and pīluparṇī; (2.4.265) pāṭā, ambaṣṭā, viddhakarṇī, sthāpanī, śreyasī, and rasā; (2.4.266) ekāṣṭīlā, pāpacelī, prācīnā, and vanatiktikā.
(2.4.267) *kaṭu*, *kaṭambharā*, *aśoka*, *rohiṇī*, *kaṭurohiṇī*;
(2.4.268) *matsyapittā*, *kṛṣṇabhedī*, *cakrāṅgī*, *śakulādanī*; (2.4.269) *ātmaguptā*, *ajahāvyā*, *aṇḍā*, *kaṇḍūrā*, *prāvṛṣāyaṇī*.
(2.4.270) *Ṛṣyaproktā*, *śūkaśimbi*, and *kapikacchu* are synonyms for *markaṭī*.
(2.4.271) *Citrā*, *upacitrā*, *nyagrodhī*, *dravantī*, *śambarī*, and *vṛśā* [are synonyms].
(2.4.272) *Pratyakśreṇī*, *sutaśreṇī*, *raṇḍā*, and *mūṣikaparṇī* [are also synonyms].
(2.4.273) *Apāmārga*, *śaikharika*, *dhāmārgava*, and *mayūraka*;
(2.4.274) *pratyakparṇī*, *keśaparṇī*, *kiṇihī*, and *kharamañjarī*;
(2.4.275) *hañjikā*, *brāhmaṇī*, *padmā*, *bhargī*, and *brāhmaṇayaṣṭikā*.
(2.4.276) *Aṅgāravallī*, *bāleyaśāka*, *barbara*, and *vardhaka*;
(2.4.277) *mañjiṣṭhā*, *vikasā*, *jiṅgī*, *samaṅgā*, and *kālameṣikā*;
(2.4.278) *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, *maṇḍīrī*, *bhaṇḍī*, and also *yojanavallī*.
(2.4.279) *yāsa*, *yavāsa*, *duḥsparśa*, *dhanvayāsa*, and *kunāśaka*;
(2.4.280) *rodanī*, *kacchurā*, *anantā*, *samudrāntā*, and *durālabhā*;
(2.4.281) *pṛśniparṇī*, *pṛthakparṇī*, *citraparṇī*, and *aṅghrivallikā*.
(2.4.282) *kroṣṭuvinnā*, *siṃhapucchī*, *kalaśī*, *dhāvanī*, and *guhā*;
(2.4.283) *nidigdhikā*, *spṛśī*, *vyāghrī*, *bṛhatī*, and *kaṇṭakārikā*;
(2.4.284) *pracodanī*, *kulī*, *kṣudrā*, *duḥsparśā*, and also *rāṣṭrikā*.
(2.4.285) Nīlī, kālā, klītakikā, grāmīṇā, and madhuparṇikā;
(2.4.286) rañjanī, śrīphalī, tutthā, droṇī, dolā, and nīlinī; (2.4.287) avalgujaḥ, somarājī, suvalli, and somavallikā.
(2.4.288) *Kālameṣī*, *kṛṣṇaphalī*, *bākucī*, and also *pūtiphalī*;
(2.4.289) *kṛṣṇā*, *upakulyā*, *vaidehī*, *māgadhī*, *capalā*, *kaṇā*, (2.4.290) *uṣaṇā*, *pippalī*, *śauṇḍī*, *kolā*, and *karipippalī*.
(2.4.291) *kapivallī* and *kolavallī* are synonyms for *śreyasī*; *vaśiraḥ* is masculine.
(2.4.292) *cavyam* and *cavikā* refer to the same plant; *kākaciñcī* and *guñjā* are synonyms for *kṛṣṇalā*.
(2.4.293) *palaṅkaṣā*, *ikṣugandhā*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, and *svādukaṇṭaka* are synonyms.

(2.4.294) Gokaṇṭaka, gokṣuraka, and also vanaśṛṅgāṭa; (2.4.295) viśvā, viṣā, prativiṣā, ativiṣā, upaviṣā, and aruṇā; (2.4.296) śṛṅgī and mahauṣadha; and furthermore, kṣīrāvī and dugdhikā are synonyms.
(2.4.297) *śatamūlī*, *bahusutā*, *abhīru*, *indīvarī*, and *varī*;
(2.4.298) *ṛṣyaproktā*, *abhīrupatrī*, and *nārāyaṇī* are synonyms for *śatāvarī*; (2.4.299) *aheru*, *pītadru*, *kālīyaka*, and *haridrava*.
(2.4.300) *Dārvī*, *pacaṃpacā*, *dāruharidrā*, and also *parjanī*;
(2.4.301) *vacā*, *ugragandhā*, *ṣaḍgranthā*, *golomī*, and *śataparvikā*;
(2.4.302) *śuklā*, *haimavatī*; while *vaidyamātṛ* and *siṃhī* are synonyms for *vāśikā*.

(2.4.303) *vṛṣa*, *aṭarūṣa*, *siṃhāsya*, *vāsaka*, and *vājidantaka*; (2.4.304) *āsphoṭā* and *girikarṇī* are synonyms for *viṣṇukrāntā* and *aparājitā*; (2.4.305) *ikṣugandhā*, *kāṇḍekṣu*, *kokilākṣa*, *ikṣuraka*, and *kṣura*.

(2.4.306) *Śāleya* may be *śītaśiva*, *chatrā*, *madhurikā*, or *misi*. (2.4.307) *Miśreyā* is also [so called]. Now, *sīhuṇḍa*, *vajra*, *snuk*, *snuhī*, and *guḍā*—(2.4.308) as well as *samantadugdhā*—are synonyms. Furthermore, *vellam*, *amoghā*, and *citrataṇḍulā* [are synonyms].
(2.4.309) *Taṇḍula* and *kṛmighna* denote *viḍaṅga*, which is both masculine and neuter. (2.4.310) *Balā* and *vāṭyālakā* [are synonyms]. *Ghaṇṭāravā* and *śaṇapuṣpikā* [are synonyms].
(2.4.311) *Mṛdvīkā*, *gostanī*, *drākṣā*, *svādvī*, and *madhurasā* [are synonyms for the grape].

(2.4.312) *sarvānubhūti*, *saralā*, *tripuṭā*, *trivṛtā*, and *trivṛt*; (2.4.313) *tribhaṇḍī* and *rocanī*; *śyāmā* and *pālindī* are synonyms for *suṣeṇikā*; (2.4.314) *kālā*, *masūravidalā*, *ardhacandrā*, and *kālameṣikā*.
(2.4.315) *Madhuka*, *klītaka*, *yaṣṭimadhuka*, and *madhuyaṣṭikā* are synonyms for liquorice.
(2.4.316) *Vidārī*, *kṣīraśuklā*, and *ikṣugandhā* refer to the same plant; however, that which is white is called *kroṣṭī*.
(2.4.317) Another variety is *kṣīravidārī*, also known as *mahāśvetā* and *ṛkṣagandhikā*.
(2.4.318) *lāṅgalī*, *śāradī*, *toyapippalī*, and *śakulādanī*;
(2.4.319) *kharāśvā*, *kāravī*, *dīpya*, *mayūra*, and *locamastaka*;
(2.4.320) *gopī*, *śyāmā*, and *śārivā*—these are synonyms for *anantā*, *utpala*, and *śārivā*.
(2.4.321) *yogya*, *ṛddhi*, *siddhi*, and *lakṣmī* are synonyms for prosperity (*vṛddhi*).
(2.4.322) *Kadalī*, *vāraṇabusā*, *rambhā*, *mocā*, and *aṃśumatphalā* are synonyms for the plantain tree.
(2.4.323) *Kāṣṭhīlā*, *mudgaparṇī*, *kākamudgā*, and *sahā* are synonyms for the mudgaparṇī plant.
Vārtākī, hiṅgulī, siṃhī, bhaṇṭākī, and duṣpradharṣiṇī;
nākulī, surasā, rāsnā, sugandhā, and gandhanākulī;
nakuleṣṭā, bhujaṃgākṣī, chatrākī, and suvahā are synonyms for it.
(2.4.327) Vidārigandhā, Aṃśumatī, Sālaparṇī, Sthirā, and Dhruvā; (2.4.328) Tuṇḍikerī, Samudrāntā, Kārpāsī, and Badarā; (2.4.329) Bhāradvājī is the wild variety; Śṛṅgī, Ṛṣabha, and Vṛṣa are synonyms.
(2.4.330) Gāṅgerukī, nāgabalā, jhaṣā, and hrasvagavedhukā;
(2.4.331) dhāmārgava is ghośaka, while mahājālī is pītaka; (2.4.332) jyotsnī, paṭolikā, jālī, nādeyī, and bhūmijambukā.
(2.4.333) *lāṅgalikī*, *agniśikhā*, *kākāṅgī*, and *kākanāsikā* are synonyms.
(2.4.334) *godhāpadī*, *suvahā*, *musālī*, and *tālamūlikā* are synonyms.
(2.4.335) *ajaśṛṅgī* and *viṣāṇī* are synonyms; likewise, *gojihvā* and *dārvikā* are identical.

(2.4.336) *tāmbūlavallī* and *tambūlī* denote the betel vine; *nāgavallī* is also used for it. Furthermore, (2.4.337) *dvijā*, *hareṇu*, *reṇukā*, *kauntī*, *kapilā*, and *bhasmagandhinī* denote the *reṇukā* plant.
(2.4.338) *elāvāluka*, *maileya*, *sugandhi*, and *harivāluka* denote the fragrant *elā* (cardamom).

(2.4.339) *vāluka* and *pālaṅkya*; *mukunda*, *kunda*, and *kunduru*; (2.4.340) *bāla*, *hrībera*, *barhiṣṭha*, *udīcya*, and *keśāmbu*; (2.4.341) *kālānusārya*, *vṛddha*, *aśmapuṣpa*, and *śītaśiva*.
Śaileya, tālaparṇī, daityā, gandhakuṭī, and murā; gandhinī, gajabhakṣyā, suvahā, surabhī, and rasā; maheraṇā, kundurukī, sallakī, and hlādinī.

(2.4.345) *Agnijvālā* and *subhikṣā* refer to *dhātakī*, also known as *dhātupuṣpikā*. (2.4.346) *Pṛthvīkā*, *candravālā*, *elā*, *niṣkuṭī*, and *bahilā* are synonyms for cardamom. (2.4.347) It is also called *sūkṣmā*, *upakuñcikā*, *tutthā*, *koraṅgī*, *tripuṭā*, and *truṭi*.

(2.4.348) *vyādhi*, *kuṣṭha*, *pāribhāvya*, *vāpya*, *pākala*, and *utpala*; (2.4.349) *śaṅkhinī* and *corapuṣpī* are synonyms; *keśinī* and *vitunnaka*; (2.4.350) *jhaṭāmalā*, *jhaṭā*, *tālī*, *śivā*, and *tāmalakī*.
(2.4.351) *Prapauṇḍarīka*, *pauṇḍarya*, then *tunna*, *kuberaka*,
(2.4.352) *kuṇi*, *kaccha*, *kāntalaka*, *nandivṛkṣa*, then *rākṣasī*, (2.4.353) *caṇḍā*, *dhanaharī*, *kṣema*, *duṣpatra*, *gaṇahāsaka*.
(2.4.354) Vyāḍāyudha, vyāghranakha, karaja, and cakrakāraka;
(2.4.355) suṣirā, vidrumalatā, kapotāṅghri, naṭī, and nalī; (2.4.356) dhamanī, añjanakeśī, hanu, and haṭṭavilāsinī.

(2.4.357) *Śukti*, *śaṅkha*, *khura*, *koladala*, *nakha*, and *āḍhakī*; (2.4.358) *kākṣī*, *mṛtsnā*, *tuvarikā*, *mṛttālaka*, and *surāṣṭraja*; (2.4.359) *kuṭannaṭa*, *dāśapura*, *vāneya*, and *paripelava*.
(2.4.360) *plavaga*, *gopura*, *gonarda*, *kaivartī*, and *mustaka*;
(2.4.361) *granthiparṇa*, *śuka*, *barha*, *puṣpa*, *sthauṇeya*, and *kukkura*; (2.4.362) *marunmālā*, *piśunā*, *spṛkkā*, *devī*, *latā*, and *laghu*.
(2.4.363) *Samudrāntā*, *vadhū*, *koṭivarṣā*, and also *laṅkopikā*;
(2.4.364) *tapasvinī*, *jaṭāmāṃsī*, *jaṭilā*, and *lomaśāmiṣī*;
(2.4.365) *tvakpatra*, *utkaṭa*, *bhṛṅga*, *tvaca*, *coca*, and *varāṅgaka*.
(2.4.366) *Karcūraka*, *drāviḍaka*, *kālpaka*, and *vedhamukhyaka* [are synonyms for a type of medicinal plant].
(2.4.367) The term *oṣadhī* (medicinal herb) is used when referring to the genus; when not referring to the genus, the word *auṣadha* (medicine/remedy) is used for everything.
(2.4.368) Vegetables such as leaves and flowers are called *śāka*; *taṇḍulīya* and *alpamāriṣa* [are synonyms for a specific herb].
Viśalyā, agniśikhā, anantā, phalinī, and śakrapuṣpikā;
dakṣagandhā, chagalāntrī, yāvegī, and vṛddhadāraka;
juṅga, brāhmī, matsyākṣī, vayaḥsthā, and somavallarī.
(2.4.372) *paṭuparṇī*, *haimavatī*, *svarṇakṣīrī*, and *himāvatī*;
(2.4.373) *hayapucchī* and *kāmbojī* are synonyms for *māṣaparṇī* and *mahāsahā*;
(2.4.374) *tuṇḍikerī*, *raktaphalā*, *bimbikā*, and *pīluparṇī* are also [names for the same plant].

(2.4.375) Barbarā, kabarī, tuṅgī, kharapuṣpā, and ajagandhikā; (2.4.376) elāparṇī, suvahā, rāsnā, and yuktarasā are synonyms for that [plant]; (2.4.377) cāṅgerī, cukrikā, dantaśaṭā, ambaṣṭhā, and amlaloṇikā are synonyms for sorrel.
*Sahasravedhī* and *cukra* are synonyms for *amlavetasa*; it is also called *śatavedhī*.
*Namaskārī*, *gaṇḍakārī*, *samaṅgā*, and *khadirā* are also [names for the same plant].
*Jīvantī*, *jīvanī*, *jīvā*, *jīvanīyā*, and *madhusravā* are synonyms for *jīvantī*.
(2.4.381) Kūrcaśīrṣa, madhuraka, śṛṅga, hrasvāṅga, and jīvaka; (2.4.382) kirātatikta, bhūnimba, anāryatikta, and then saptalā;
(2.4.383) vimalā, sātalā, bhūriphenā, and also carmakaṣā.
(2.4.384) Vāyasolī, Svādurasā, and Vayaḥsthā; then Makūlaka (2.4.385), Nikumbha, Dantikā, Pratyakśreṇī, and Udumbaraparṇī; (2.4.386) Ajamodā, Ugragandhā, Brahmadarbhā, and Yavānikā.
(2.4.387) At its root are *puṣkara*, *kāśmīra*, and *padmapatra* in the *pauṣkara* group;
(2.4.388) *avyathā*, *aticarā*, *padmā*, *cāraṭī*, and *padmacāriṇī*;
(2.4.389) *kāmpilya*, *karkaśa*, *candra*, *raktāṅga*, and also *rocanī*.
(2.4.390) *prapunnāḍa* is *eḍagaja*, *dadrughna*, and *cakramardaka*;
(2.4.391) it is also called *padmāṭa* and *uraṇa*. *Palāṇḍu* is *sukandaka*; (2.4.392) when green, it is *latārka* and *dudruma*. Furthermore, it is *mahauṣadha*.
Garlic, *gṛñjana*, *ariṣṭa*, *mahākanda*, and *rasonaka* [are synonyms].
*Punarnavā*, however, is called *śothaghnī*; *vitunna* is *suniṣaṇṇaka*. *Vāstūka* is *śītala*; *aparājitā* is also *śaṇaparṇī*.

(2.4.396) *pārāvatāṅghri*, *kaṭabhī*, *paṇyā*, and *jyotiṣmatī* are synonyms for the creeper. (2.4.397) *vārṣikā*, *trāyamāṇā*, *trāyantī*, and *balabhadrikā* are synonyms for the plant. (2.4.398) *viṣvaksenapriyā*, *gṛṣṭi*, *vārāhī*, and *badarā* are also [synonyms].
(2.4.399) *mārkava* is *bhṛṅgarāja*, while *kākamācī* is *vāyasī*. (2.4.400) *śatapuṣpā*, *sitacchatrā*, *aticchatrā*, *madhurā*, and *misi* [are synonyms].
(2.4.401) *avākpuṣpī* and *kāravī* [are synonyms], while *saraṇā* is *prasāriṇī*.
(2.4.402) In that [category] are *kaṭaṃbhara*, *rājabalā*, and also *bhadrabalā*.
(2.4.403) *Janī*, *jatūkā*, *rajanī*, *jatukṛt*, and *cakravartinī*;
(2.4.404) *saṃsparśā*; then *śaṭī*, *gandhamūlī*, and also *ṣaḍgranthikā*.
(2.4.405) *karcūra* is also *palāśa*; now, *kāravella* is *kaṭhillaka*.
(2.4.406) *suṣavī* also; now, *kulaka*, *patola*, *tiktaka*, and *paṭu* [are synonyms].
(2.4.407) *kūṣmāṇḍaka* is *karkāru*; *urvāru* and *karkaṭī* are feminine.

(2.4.408) *Ikṣvāku* is the bitter gourd (*kaṭutumbī*); *tumbī* and *alābū* are both synonyms for the bottle gourd. (2.4.409) *Citrā*, *gavākṣī*, and *goḍumbā* refer to the same plant; *viśālā* is the *indravāruṇī* (cucumber).
(2.4.410) *Arśoghna*, *sūraṇa*, and *kanda* are synonyms for the arrow-root; *gaṇḍīra* is the *samaṣṭhilā*.

(2.4.411) *Kālambyupodikā* is feminine; *mūlaka* and *hilamocikā* [are also feminine]. (2.4.412) *Vāstuka* and others are varieties of potherbs (*śāka*); *dūrvā*, however, is *śataparvikā*. (2.4.413) It is also called *sahasravīryā* and *bhārgavī*; furthermore, it is *ruhā* and *anantā*, and when white, it is that same [term].

(2.4.414) *golomī*, *śatavīryā*, *gaṇḍālī*, and *śakulākṣakā*; (2.4.415) *kuruvinda*, *meghanāman*, *mustā*, and *mustaka*—the last being not feminine; (2.4.416) *bhadramustaka*, *gundrā*, *cūḍālā*, and *cakraloccaṭā*.
(2.4.417) *vaṃśa* [denotes] bamboo; [its synonyms are] *tvaksāra*, *karmāra*, *tvaci-sāra*, *tṛṇadhvaja*.
(2.4.418) *śataparvan*, *yavaphala*, *veṇu*, *maskara*, and *tejana* [are also names for bamboo]. (2.4.419) Those bamboos that resound when shaken by the wind are called *kīcaka*.
(2.4.420) *granthi* is a joint (*parva*, *paru*); *gundra* is *tejanaka* and *śara*. (2.4.421) *naḍa* is *dhamana* and *poṭagala*; furthermore, *kāśa* is not feminine.
(2.4.422) *ikṣugandhā* and *poṭagala* [are synonyms]; however, *balvaja* is used in the masculine plural.
(2.4.423) *Rasāla* is sugarcane; its varieties include *puṇḍraka*, *kāntāraka*, and others.
(2.4.424) *Vīraṇa* and *vīratara* refer to the same plant; its root is called *uśīra*, which is used as a neuter noun.
(2.4.425) *Abhaya*, *nalada*, *sevya*, *amṛṇāla*, and *jalāśaya* are synonyms for the lotus stalk.
(2.4.426) *Lāmajjaka* is light and cooling, beneficial for those suffering from burns and for walking on paths of brick.
(2.4.427) *Naḍa* and others, as well as *garmut*, *śyāmāka*, and so forth, are grasses.
(2.4.428) *Kuśa*, *kutha*, *darbha*, *pavitra*, and *kattṛṇa* are not feminine [i.e., they are masculine]. 980
(2.4.429) *paurasaugandhika*, *dhyāmadaiva*, *jagdhakara*, and *karoiṣa*;
(2.4.430) *chatrāticchatra*, *pālaghna*, *mālātṛṇaka*, and *bhūstṛṇa*;
(2.4.431) *śaṣpa* is young grass; *ghāsa* is fodder; *yavasa* is grass; and *arjuna* is [also] grass.
(2.4.432) A collection of grasses is *tṛṇyā*, while a collection of reeds is *naḍyā*.
(2.4.433) The palm tree is called *tṛṇarāja*; the coconut is *nālikera* and also *lāṅgalī*.
(2.4.434) The betel nut tree is *ghoṇṭā*, *pūga*, *kramuka*, and *guvāka*; its fruit is *khapura*.

(2.4.435) Phala, udvega, and these three together with hintāla; (2.4.436) kharjūra, ketakī, tālī, and kharjurī are the grass-trees. Thus ends the section on forest plants. Now begins the section on lions and other animals.

(2.4.437) Siṃha (lion), mṛgendra (lord of beasts), pañcāsya (five-faced), haryakṣa (tawny-eyed), kesarī (maned), hari (the tawny one); (2.4.438) kaṇṭīrava (throat-roarer), mṛgāri (enemy of deer), mṛgadṛṣṭi (deer-eyed), mṛgāśana (deer-eater); (2.4.439) puṇḍarīka (lotus-like), pañcanakha (five-clawed), citrakāya (variegated-bodied), mṛgadviṣ (deer-hater).
(2.4.440) *Śārdūla* and *dvīpin* refer to the tiger; *tarakṣu* is the hyena, also known as *mṛgādana*.
(2.4.441) *Varāha*, *sūkara*, *ghṛṣṭi*, *kola*, *potrī*, *kiri*, and *kiṭi* refer to the boar.
(2.4.442) It is also called *daṃṣṭrī*, *ghoṇī*, *stabdharomā*, *kroḍa*, and *bhūdāra*.
(2.4.443) *kapi*, *plavaṅgama*, *plavaga*, *śākhāmṛga*, and *valīmukha*;

(2.4.444) *markaṭa*, *vānara*, *kīśa*, and *vanaukā* [are synonyms for monkey]. Now, *bhalluka*—(2.4.445) *ṛkṣa*, *acchabhalla*, and *bhallūka* [refer to the bear]; *gaṇḍaka*, *khaḍga*, and *khaḍgin* [refer to the rhinoceros].
(2.4.446) *lulāya*, *mahiṣa*, *vāha*, *dviṣat*, *kāsara*, and *sairibha* [are synonyms for] buffalo.
(2.4.447) In the feminine, *śivā*, *bhūrimāya*, *gomāyu*, and *mṛgadhūrtaka* [are synonyms for] jackal.
(2.4.448) *śṛgāla*, *vañcaka*, *kroṣṭu*, *pheru*, *pherava*, and *jambuka* [are also synonyms for] jackal.
(2.4.449) *utpibidāla*, *mārjāra*, *vṛṣadaṃśaka*, and *ākhubhuk* are synonyms for a cat;
(2.4.450) *gaudhera*, *gaudhāra*, and *gaudheya* are the three names for the offspring of a *godhikā* (a type of lizard);
(2.4.451) *śvāvit* is a porcupine; its quill is called *śalya*, and the individual quill is called *śalalī*, *śalala*, and *śala*.
(2.4.452) *vātapramī* is a wind-animal; *kokas* is a forest-deer (*īhāmṛga*), while *vṛka* is a wolf.
(2.4.453) For a deer (*mṛga*), there are *kuraṅga*, *vātāyu*, *hariṇa*, and *ajinayoni*.
(2.4.454) *Aiṇeya* is the skin of a female deer (*eṇī*); *aiṇa* is the skin of a male deer (*eṇa*). Both [terms] apply to all three genders.
(2.4.455) *Kadalī*, *kandalī*, *cīna*, *camūru*, and *priyaka*;
(2.4.456) and *samūru*—these are the deer that serve as sources of skins; (2.4.457) *kṛṣṇasāra*, *ruru*, *nyaṅku*, *raṅku*, *śambara*, and *rauhiṣa*.
(2.4.458) *gokarṇa*, *pṛṣata*, *eṇa*, *ṛśya*, *rohit*, and *camara* are deer;
(2.4.459) *gandharva*, *śarabha*, *rāma*, *sṛmara*, *gavaya*, and *śaśa*; (2.4.460) these and others, such as the lions among beasts and the cattle and so forth, are the species of animals. 1010.
(2.4.461) A digger who goes downwards is a *khanaka*; a wolf is *vṛka*; a rat is *pundhvaja* and *undura*.
(2.4.462) *Unduru*, *mūṣaka*, and *ākhu* also mean rat; *girikā* is a young mouse (*bālamūṣikā*).
(2.4.463) *Cucundarī* and *gandhamūṣī* are also names for it; a long-bodied mouse is simply called *mūṣikā*.
(2.4.464) *Saraṭa* and *kṛkalāsa* denote a chameleon; *musalī* and *gṛhagodhikā* denote a house-lizard.
(2.4.465) *Lūtā*, *strī*, *tantuvāya*, *ūrṇanābha*, and *markaṭaka* are synonymous terms for a spider.
(2.4.466) *Nīlaṅgu* denotes a worm; both *karṇajalaukā* and *śatapadī* denote a centipede.
(2.4.467) *vṛścikaḥ* is a scorpion; *ali* and *druma* refer to the scorpion. (2.4.468) *Pārāvata* is the turtle-dove (*kalarava*); *kapota* is the pigeon.
Then, *śaśādana*, (2.4.469) *patrī*, and *śyena* denote the hawk. *Ulūka*, however, refers to the crow’s enemy (*vāyasārāti*) and the owl (*pecaka*).

(2.4.470) *divāndhaḥ*, *kauśikaḥ*, *ghūkaḥ*, *divābhītaḥ*, and *niśāṭanaḥ* are names for the owl; (2.4.471) *vyāghrāṭaḥ* and *bharadvājaḥ* refer to the bharadvāja bird, while *khañjarīṭaḥ* and *khañjanaḥ* refer to the wagtail; (2.4.472) *lohapṛṣṭhaḥ* and *kaṅkaḥ* refer to the heron, and *cāṣaḥ* and *kikīdiviḥ* refer to the blue jay.
(2.4.473) The *kaliṅga*, *bhṛṅga*, and *dhūmyāṭa* are [names for the same bird]; then there is the *śatapatraka*.
(2.4.474) The *dārvāghāṭa*; then the *sāraṅga*, *stokaka*, and *cātaka* are synonyms.
(2.4.475) The *kṛkavāku*, *tāmracūḍa*, *kukkuṭa*, and *caraṇāyudha* [are names for the cock].
The *caṭaka* is the *kalaviṅka*; its female is the *caṭakā*.
Their male offspring is the *cāṭakaira*, and their female offspring is likewise called a *caṭakā*.
The *karkareṭu* and *kareṭu* are [names for the same bird]; the *kṛkaṇa* and *krakara* are synonyms.
(2.4.479) *vanapriyaḥ*, *parabhṛtaḥ*, *kokilaḥ*, and also *pikaḥ* [denote the cuckoo].
(2.4.480) Regarding the crow, however: *kākaḥ*, *karaṭaḥ*, *ariṣṭaḥ*, *balipuṣṭaḥ*, *sakṛtprajaḥ*, (2.4.481) *dhvāṅkṣaḥ*, *ātmaghoṣaḥ*, *parabhṛt* (?), *balibhuk*, and *vāyasaḥ* [are its synonyms].
He is also known as Cirañjīvī, Ekadṛṣṭi, and Maukuli.
Droṇakāka is the same as Kākola; Dātyūha is the same as Kālakaṇṭhaka.
Ātāpi and Cilla are synonyms for Dākṣāyya; Gṛdhra is the vulture; and Kīra and Śuka are synonymous. 1030
(2.4.485) *Kruṅ* is the *krauñca*; then *baka* is the heron, and *kahva* is the *puṣkarāhva*, which is the *sārasa*.
(2.4.486) *Koka* is the *cakra*, also known as *cakravāka*, which is named after the wheel of a chariot (*rathāṅga*). (2.4.487) *Kādamba* is the *kalahaṃsa*; *utkrośa* and *kurara* are synonyms.
(2.4.488) The *haṃsa* birds have white wings, possess webbed feet, and dwell on Lake Mānasa. (2.4.489) Those with red beaks and legs are the *rājahaṃsa*.
(2.4.490) Those with soiled [beaks and legs] are the *mallikākṣa*, while those with black [beaks and legs] are the *dhārtarāṣṭra*.
(2.4.491) *Śarārī*, *āṭī*, and *āḍī* denote the crane (*balākā*), as does *bisakaṇṭhikā*.
(2.4.492) *Varaṭā* is the female of the swan (*haṃsa*); *lakṣmaṇā* is the female of the *sārasa* crane.
(2.4.493) *Jatukā*, *ajinapatrā*, *paroṣṇī*, and *tailapāyikā* denote the *khañjarīṭa* (wagtail).
(2.4.494) *Varvaṇā* and *makṣikā* mean a fly; *saraghā* and *madhumakṣikā* mean a honeybee.
(2.4.495) *Pataṅgikā* and *puttikā* refer to a gnat; *daṃśa*, however, refers to a forest fly (a mosquito).
(2.4.496) *Daṃśī* is a small variety of that same species; *gandholī* and *varaṭā* (masculine and feminine) denote the gadfly.
(2.4.497) *bhṛṅgārī*, *jhīrukā*, *cīrī*, and *jhillikā* are synonyms for the cricket.
(2.4.498) *pataṅga* and *śalabha* are synonyms for the locust; *khadyota* and *jyotiriṅgaṇa* refer to the firefly.
(2.4.499) *madhuvrata*, *madhukara*, *madhulih*, and *madhupa* denote the bee.
(2.4.500) The bee is called *dvirepha*, *puṣpaliṭ*, *bhṛṅga*, *ṣaṭpada*, and *bhramarālaya*.
(2.4.501) The peacock is called *mayūra*, *barhiṇa*, *barhī*, *nīlakaṇṭha*, and *bhujaṃgabhuk*.
(2.4.502) It is also called *śikhāvala*, *śikhī*, *kekī*, and *meghanādānulāsyin*.
(2.4.503) *kekā* is the cry of a peacock; *candraka* and *mecaka* are synonyms for its eye-like spots.
(2.4.504) *śikhā*, *cūḍā*, and *śikhaṇḍa* denote the crest; *piccha* and *barha* are neuter terms for the feathers. (2.4.505) *khaga*, *vihaṅga*, *vihaga*, *vihaṅgama*, and *vihāyas* refer to a bird.
(2.4.506) *śakunti*, *pakṣin*, *śakuni*, *śakunta*, *śakuna*, and *dvija*;
(2.4.507) *patatrin*, *patrin*, *pataga*, *patat*, *patraratha*, and *aṇḍaja*;
(2.4.508) *nagauka*, *vājin*, *vikira*, *vivikira*, and *patatrin*.
(2.4.509) Born from nests are the Garuḍas, who fly through the sky seeking to soar; (2.4.510) their specific varieties are the Hārīta, Madgu, Kāraṇḍava, Plava,
(2.4.511) Tittiri, Kukkubha, Lāva, Jīvañjīva, and Koraka.

(2.4.512) *koyaṣṭika*, *ṭiṭṭibhaka*, *vartaka*, *vartikā*, and others; (2.4.513) *garut*, *pakṣa*, and *chada* denote a wing; *patra* and *patatra* denote a feather or wing; and *tanūruha* denotes a feather.
(2.4.514) *pakṣati* and *pakṣamūla* denote the root of a wing; *cañcu* and *troṭi* both denote the beak, and both are feminine.
(2.4.515) *Praḍīna*, *uḍḍīna*, and *saṃḍīna* are these terms for the flight-movements of birds.
(2.4.516) *Peśī* and *kośa* refer to the egg-casing; when two [syllables] are omitted, the words are *aṇḍa*, *kulāya*, and *nīḍa* (the latter being neuter).
(2.4.517) *Pota*, *pāka*, *arbhaka*, *ḍimbha*, *pṛthuka*, *śāvaka*, and *śiśu* all denote a young child.

(2.4.518) *Strī* and *pumsau* form a pair (*mithunam*); *dvandvam*, *yugmam*, *yugulam*, and *yugam* denote a couple. (2.4.519) In the sense of a collection (*samūha*), there are *nivaha*, *vyūha*, *sandoha*, *visara*, *vraja*, (2.4.520) *stoma*, *ogha*, *nikara*, *vrāta*, *vāra*, *saṃghāta*, and *saṃcaya*.

(2.4.521) A collection (*samudāya*), an assemblage (*samudaya*), and a multitude (*gaṇa*) are synonyms for a group; (2.4.522) while in the feminine gender, the terms *saṃhati*, *vṛnda*, *nikuramba*, and *kadambaka* denote a cluster.
(2.4.523) Varieties of clusters include *varga* when the members are equal, whereas *saṃgha* and *sārtha* refer to groups consisting of living beings.
(2.4.524) A *kula* or *yūtha* refers to a group of animals of the same species; these terms are both masculine and neuter.
(2.4.525) For domestic animals, such a gathering is called a *samaja*, whereas for others it is a *samāja*; furthermore, for those who share the same religious duties (*sadharmiṇ*), it is a *nikāya*.
(2.4.526) A heap or pile is a *puñja* or *rāśi*; however, an *utkara*, *kūṭa*, and *astriyām* (meaning "not feminine") also denote a mound or heap.

(2.4.527) *kāpota*, *śauka*, *māyūra*, *taittira*, and so forth, belong to that group. (2.4.528) Birds and beasts attached to houses are called *cheka*; they are also called *gṛhyaka*. Thus ends the section on lions and other [beasts].
(2.5.529) *manuṣya*, *mānuṣa*, *martya*, *manuja*, *mānava*, *nara*. Now begins the section on humans (2.5.530): *pumāṃs*, *pañcajana*, *puruṣa*, *pūruṣa*, *nara* [are synonyms].
(2.5.531) Strī, yoṣit, abalā, yoṣā, nārī, sīmantinī, and vadhū; (2.5.532) pratīpadarśinī, vāmā, vanitā, and likewise mahilā; (2.5.533) as specific terms:
aṅganā, bhīruḥ, kāminī, and vāmalocanā.
(2.5.534) *Pramadā*, *māninī*, *kāntā*, *lalanā*, and *nitambinī*;

(2.5.535) *sundarī*, *ramaṇī*, and *rāmā* [are synonyms for woman]. That same woman when prone to anger is called *kopanā* or *bhāminī*. (2.5.536) *Varārohā*, *mattakāśinī*, *uttamā*, and *varavarṇinī* [also denote a beautiful woman].
(2.5.537) The consecrated queen is the *mahiṣī*; other royal wives are *bhoginī*s.

(2.5.538) A wife is a *patnī*, a *pāṇigṛhītī*, or a *dvitīyā* (second [partner]); she is also a *sahadharmiṇī*. (2.5.539) A wife is a *bhāryā* or a *jāyā*; in the plural masculine, they are *dārāḥ*; while a woman who has a family is a *kuṭumbinī*.

(2.5.540) *Purandhrī* refers to a woman of good character; she is also called *satī*, *sādhvī*, and *pativratā*. (2.5.541) A woman who has been superseded by a co-wife is called *kṛtasāpatnikā*; one who has been married after another is *adhyūḍhā*; and one who has been superseded [by a younger wife] is *adhivinā*. (2.5.542) A woman who chooses her own husband is *svayaṃvarā* and *patiṃvarā*; she is also called *varyā*. Furthermore, a woman of noble family is a *kulastrī* or a *kulapālikā*.

(2.5.543) A maiden (*kanyā*) is a girl (*kumārī*); *gaurī*, however, refers to one who is naked and has not yet reached puberty. (2.5.544) One who has seen her menses is called *madhyamā*; *taruṇī* and *yuvati* are synonymous terms for a young woman. (2.5.545) *Snuṣā*, *janī*, and *vadhū* are equivalent; *ciriṇṭī*, on the other hand, refers to a married woman whose husband is living.
(2.5.546) One who possesses desire is *kāmukā*; one who longs for a male is *vṛṣasyantī*, a lustful woman (*kāmukī*).
(2.5.547) She who goes to an appointment seeking her lover is called *abhisārikā*.
(2.5.548) A wanton woman is *puṃścalī*, *dharṣiṇī*, *bandhakī*, *asatī*, *kulaṭā*, or *itvarī*.
(2.5.549) A woman who acts according to her own will is called *svairiṇī*, and one who is unchaste is *pāṃsulā*. One who lacks a child is *aśiśvī*.

(2.5.550) One who has neither husband nor son is *avīrā*. *Viśvastā* and *avidhavā* are synonymous terms for a widow. (2.5.551) *Āli*, *sakhī*, and *vayasyā* denote a female friend. *Pativatnī* refers to a woman whose husband is living.
(2.5.552) *Vṛddhā* means an old woman; *paliknī* means one with grey hair. *Prājñī* means a wise woman; *prājñā* and *dhīmatī* mean an intelligent woman.

(2.5.553) *Śūdrī* may be the wife of a Śūdra, or it may denote that very caste itself. (2.5.554) *Ābhīrī* and *mahāśūdrī* are the same in both their application as a caste name and as a term for a woman through her union with a man of that caste.
(2.5.555) An *āryā* woman who is herself noble is called *āryā*; likewise, a *kṣatriyā* woman is called *kṣatriyāṇī*.

(2.5.556) An *upādhyāya* is also [called] *upādhyāyī*, and an *ācārya* is also [called] *ācāryā* by virtue of her own status. (2.5.557) But in the sense of a relationship with a male (*puṃyoga*), she is *ācāryānī*; likewise, she is *aryī* or *kṣatriyī*.
(2.5.558) *Upādhyāyā* and *upādhyāyī* refer to a female preceptor; a *poṭā* is a woman possessing the characteristics of both male and female.
(2.5.559) A *vīrapatnī*, *vīrabhāryā*, and *vīramātā* are synonyms for a mother of heroes; however, *vīrasūḥ* specifically denotes one who has given birth to a hero.
(2.5.560) A woman who has given birth is called *jātāpatyā*, *prajātā*, *prasūtā*, and *prasūtikā*.
(2.5.561) A naked woman is a *koṭavī*; a female messenger and a go-between are synonyms (*saṃcārikā*).
(2.5.562) A widow who wears saffron-colored garments and is somewhat advanced in age is a *kātyāyanī*.
(2.5.563) A *sairandhrī* is one who resides in another's house, is independent, and performs crafts.
(2.5.564) An *asiknī* is an unmarried female servant who moves about within the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*).

(2.5.565) A courtesan is called a *gaṇikā*, a *veśyā*, or a *rūpājīvā*; furthermore, when she is honored by people, she is known as a *vāramukhyā*. (2.5.566) A procuress is a *kuṭṭanī* and a *śambhalī*; these two are synonymous.
A female fortune-teller is called *vipraśnikā*, *īkṣaṇikā*, or *daivajñā*.
A woman in her menses is called *rajasvalā*, *strīdharmiṇī*, *avirā*, *ātreyī*, *malinī*, *puṣpavatī*, *ṛtumatī*, *udakyā*; and the menstrual flow itself is termed *rajaḥ*, *puṣpa*, or *ārtava*.
(2.5.570) *śraddhāluḥ* means full of faith; *dohadavatī* means having pregnancy-longings; *niṣkalā* means devoid of menses;
(2.5.571) *āpannasattvā*, *gurviṇī*, *antarvatnī*, and *garbhiṇī* all mean pregnant;
(2.5.572) the collective term for a group of courtesans and the like is *gāṇikyam*; *gārbhiṇam* refers to a group of pregnant women; and *yauvatam* refers to a group of young women.
(2.5.573) A *punarbhū* is a remarried woman; her husband is called a *didhiṣū*. (2.5.574) That twice-born man whose wife is such a woman is an *agredidhiṣū*.
(2.5.575) A son born of an unmarried girl (*kanyakā*) is a *kānīna*; furthermore, a son of a fortunate woman (*subhagā*) is a *saubhāgya*.

(2.5.576) *Saubhāgineya* refers to the son of a fortunate woman; *pārastraiṇeya*, however, refers to the son of another's wife. (2.5.577) *Paitṛṣvaseya* and *paitṛṣvasrīya* refer to the son of a father’s sister.
(2.5.578) Likewise, the son of a mother’s sister is [called] *mātṛṣvasrīya*; and the son born of a stepmother is *vaimātreya*.

(2.5.579) Now, the son of an unchaste woman may be called *bāndhakineya* or *bandhula*. (2.5.580) He is also called *kaulaṭera* or *kaulateya*. But if she is a chaste (*satī*) beggar-woman (*bhikṣukī*), then her son is called *kaulaṭineya* or *kaulateya*.

(2.5.582) *Ātmaja*, *tanaya*, *sūnu*, *suta*, and *putra* [are synonyms for son]. However, these same terms, when used in the feminine, (2.5.583) they say, denote a daughter. *Apatya*, *toka*, and both of these [terms] apply equally to both [son and daughter]. (2.5.584) When born of one's own [wife], he is called *aurasa* or *aurasya*. *Tāta*, however, means progenitor (*janaka*) or father (*pitṛ*).
(2.5.585) *Janayitrī*, *prasūḥ*, *mātā*, *jananī* mean mother; *bhaginī*, *svasā* mean sister.
(2.5.586) *Nanāndā* is the husband’s sister; *naptrī*, *pautrī*, *sutātmajā* mean granddaughter.
(2.5.587) The wives of one's brothers are called *yātaraḥ* among themselves.
(2.5.588) *Prajāvatī* is a brother’s wife; *mātulānī* and *mātulī* are both terms for a maternal uncle’s wife.
(2.5.589) The mother of a husband or a wife is called *śvaśrū*; the father of those two is *śvaśura*.
(2.5.590) A father’s brother is *pitṛvya*; a mother’s brother is *mātula*.
(2.5.591) The brothers of a wife's husband are called *śyāla*; the husband's younger brother is *devṛ* and the elder brother is *devara*.
(2.5.592) A sister's son is *svasrīya*, and a daughter's husband is *jamātṛ*.
(2.5.593) A father's father is *pitāmaha*; his father is *prapitāmaha*.
(2.5.594) Likewise, the mother’s maternal grandfather and so forth are *sapiṇḍas* and *sanābhis*.
(2.5.595) *Samānodarya*, *sodarya*, *sagarbhya*, and *sahaja* are synonyms.
(2.5.596) *Sagotra*, *bāndhava*, *jñāti*, *bandhu*, *sva*, and *svajana* are also synonyms.

(2.5.597) *Jñāteya* and *bandhutā* denote, respectively, their kinship and their group; (2.5.598) *dhava*, *priya*, *pati*, and *bhartṛ* mean husband; *jāra* and *upapati* are synonyms for paramour; (2.5.599) one born of a paramour while the husband is alive is called *kuṇḍa*, but if the husband is dead, he is called *golaka*.
(2.5.600) *bhrātrīya*, *bhrātṛja*, and both the brother and sister are called *bhrātarau*.
(2.5.601) Mother and father are called *mātāpitarau*, *pitarau*, *mātarapitarau*, and *prasūjanayitārau*.
(2.5.602) Mother-in-law and father-in-law are called *śvaśurau*; son and daughter are called *putrau*.
(2.5.603) *daṃpatī*, *jaṃpatī*, *jāyāpatī*, and *bhāryāpatī*—these are terms for a husband and wife.

(2.5.604) *Garbhāśaya* means the womb; it is also called *jarāyu* and *ulba*. *Kalala* refers to the embryo in its earliest stage and is not feminine. (2.5.605) *Sūtimāsa* is the month of birth; *garbha* and *bhrūṇa* are synonymous terms for the fetus.

(2.5.606) A third gender is *śaṇḍha*, *klība*, *paṇḍa*, or *napuṃsaka*. (2.5.607) *Śiśutva*, *śaiśava*, and *bālya* denote childhood; *tāruṇya* and *yauvana* denote youth; they are synonymous. (2.5.608) *Sthāvira* denotes old age, as does *vārdhaka*, which may also refer to a group of elders.
(2.5.609) *Palita* is the whiteness of hair and so forth caused by old age; *visrasā* and *jarā* both mean aging.
(2.5.610) An infant is called *uttānaśayā*, *ḍimbha*, *stanapa*, and *stanandhayī*.
(2.5.611) A child is a *māṇavaka*; one who has reached maturity is *vayastha*, *taruṇa*, and *yuvan*.
(2.5.612) *Pravayas*, *sthavira*, *vṛddha*, *jīna*, *jīrṇa*, and *jaran* denote an old man.
(2.5.613) *Varṣīyān*, *daśamī*, *jyāyān*, *pūrvaja*, *agrya*, and *agraja* denote an elder brother.
(2.5.614) For one born later, there are *kaniṣṭha*, *yavīyas*, *avaraja*, and *anuja*.
(2.5.615) *amāṃsa* means lean, weak, or emaciated; *balavat*, *māṃsala*, and *aṃsala* mean strong or fleshy.
(2.5.616) *tundila*, *tundibha*, *tundī*, *bṛhatkukṣi*, and *picaṇḍila* refer to one who has a large belly.
(2.5.617) *avaṭīṭa*, *avanāṭa*, and *avabhraṭa* refer to one with a sunken nose.
(2.5.618) Keśava, keśika, and keśin denote one with hair; valina and valibha are synonyms for one with wrinkles.
(2.5.619) One with deficient limbs is called apogaṇḍa; kharva, hrasva, and vāmana denote a dwarf.
(2.5.620) One with a crooked nose is kharaṇas or kharaṇāḥ; one who has lost his nose is vigra.
One with a prominent nose is *khuraṇas* or *khuraṇasa*; one whose knees are far apart is *prajñu*.

(622) One with raised knees is *ūrdhvajñu* or *ūrdhvajānu*; one with joined knees is *saṃjñu*. (623) One who is deaf is *eḍa*; one who is hunchbacked is *gaḍula*; and one with a deformed hand is *kuṇi*.

(2.5.624) *pṛśni* refers to one with small body hair; *śroṇa* means lame; *muṇḍa* refers to one who has been shaven. (2.5.625) *valira* refers to one with squinting eyes; *khoḍa* refers to one who is lame; *khañja* is used in three genders for those aged or infirm. (2.5.626) *jaḍula*, *kālaka*, *piplu*, *tilaka*, and *tilakālaka* refer to a mole or dark spot on the skin.
(2.5.627) *Anāmaya* means health; *cikitsā* is the treatment of illness.
(2.5.628) *Bheṣaja*, *auṣadha*, *bhaiṣajya*, *agada*, and *jāyu* are synonyms for medicine.
(2.5.629) *Ruk*, *rujā*, *upatāpa*, *roga*, *vyādhi*, *gada*, and *āmaya* are feminine terms for disease.

(2.5.630) Consumption (*kṣayaḥ*), wasting (*śoṣaḥ*), and *yakṣmā*; catarrh (*pratiśyāyaḥ*) is *pīnasaḥ*. (2.5.631) A woman [is called] *strī*; sneezing is *kṣut*, *kṣutam*, or *kṣavaḥ* (masculine); cough (*kāsaḥ*) is *kṣavathuḥ* (masculine).
(2.5.632) Swelling is *śophaḥ*, *śvayathuḥ*, or *śothaḥ*; cracking of the feet is *vipādikā*.
(2.5.633) *kilāsa* and *sidhma* denote leucoderma; *kacchu*, *pāma*, *pāmā*, and *vicarcikā* denote scabies.
(2.5.634) *kaṇḍū*, *kharjū*, and *kaṇḍūyā* denote itching; *visphoṭa* and *piṭaka* (in the feminine) denote pustules.
(2.5.635) *vraṇa* (not feminine) denotes a wound; *īrma* and *aru* (neuter) denote a sore; *nāḍīvraṇa* (masculine) denotes a sinus ulcer.
(2.5.636) *Koṭha* is a circular skin eruption; *kuṣṭha* and *śvitra* are types of leprosy and vitiligo; *durnāmaka* and *arśas* refer to hemorrhoids.
(2.5.637) *Ānāha* is constipation or obstruction; *nibandha* is the same; *grahaṇī-ruj* and *pravāhikā* refer to dysentery or chronic diarrhea.
(2.5.638) *Pracchardikā*, *vamis*, and *vamathu* are synonyms for vomiting; *pracchardikā* and *vamis* are feminine, while *vamathu* is masculine.

(2.5.639) The varieties of disease are abscess (*vidradhi*), female genital disorders (*strī*), fever (*jvara*), urinary disorders (*meha*), fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṇḍara*), elephantiasis (*ślīpada*), "foot-mound" (*pādavalmīka*), and hair-loss (*keśaghna*), which is *indraluptaka*.
(2.5.641) Stone (*aśmarī*) and dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*) belong to the preceding group; [the terms] up to semen (*śukra*) apply to all three genders.

(2.5.642) A remover of disease, a healer, a physician, a vaidya, and a practitioner of medicine; (2.5.643) one who is healthy, free from illness, fit, or recovered is called *ullāgha*, meaning one who has emerged from disease;
(2.5.644) one who is sick, ill, or suffering from malady is called *glāna*, *glāsnu*, *āmayāvin*, *vikṛta*, *vyādhita*, or *apaṭu*.
(2.5.645) *Ātura*, *abhyamita*, and *abhyānta* are synonyms for one who is afflicted by illness; *pāmana* and *kacchura* are equal [terms] for one with scabies.
(2.5.646) One suffering from ringworm (*dadru*) is called *dadruṇa* or *dadrurogī*; one possessed of the disease of hemorrhoids (*arśas*) is *arśasa*.
(2.5.647) One suffering from wind-disease (*vāta*) is *vātakī* or *vātarogī*; one with dysentery (*atisāra*) is *sātisāra* or *atisārakī*.
(2.5.648) *culla*, *cilla*, and *pilla* are used for one with moist eyes; these [terms] also apply when the eyes themselves are moist.
(2.5.649) *unmatta* refers to one possessed by madness (*unmāda*); *śleṣmala*, *śleṣmaṇa*, and *kaphī* refer to one characterized by phlegm (*śleṣman*).
(2.5.650) *nyubja* refers to one bent by disease; *tundila* and *tundi* refer to one with a protruding navel.
(2.5.651) *vilāsī*, *sidhmalaḥ*, *andhaḥ*, *adṛk*, *mūrcchālaḥ*; *mūrtaḥ*, *mūrcchitaḥ*.
(2.5.652) *śukram*, *tejaḥ*, *retaḥ*; also *bījam*, *vīryam*, *indriyam*.
(2.5.653) *māyuḥ*, *pittam*, *kaphaḥ*, *śleṣmā*; in the feminine, however, *tvak* [is used] for the skin, and *asṛgdharā* for the blood-bearer.
(2.5.654) *piśita*, *tarasa*, *māṃsa*, *palala*, *kravya*, and *āmiṣa* are synonyms for raw flesh. (2.5.655) *Uttapta* refers to dried meat; it is called *vallūra*, which has three genders.
(2.5.656) For blood, the terms are *asṛj*, *lohita*, *āsra*, *rakta*, *kṣataja*, and *śoṇita*.

(2.5.657) *bukkāgramāṃsa* (the flesh at the top of the throat), *hṛdaya* (heart), *hṛnmedas* (heart-fat), *vapā* (omentum), and *vasā* (muscle-fat); (2.5.658) the vein at the back of the neck is *manyā*; *nāḍī*, *dhamani*, and *śirā* (vein); (2.5.659) *tilaka* (the liver), *kloma* (the lungs), *mastiṣka* (the brain), *gorda* (the marrow), *kiṭṭa* (excrement), and *mala* (impurity)—these are not feminine.
(2.5.660) *Antra* is the intestine; *purītat* and *gulma* are synonyms for the small intestine, while *plīhā* (the spleen) is masculine.
Then, *vasnasā*, *snāyu*, and *striyām* refer to the sinew or tendon. (2.5.661–662) *Kālakhaṇḍa* and *yakṛt* are both neuter terms for the liver.
*Sṛṇikā*, *syandanī*, and *lālā* denote saliva. *Dūṣikā* is the impurity or secretion of the eyes.
The impurity of the nose is *siṅghāṇa* or *piñjūṣa*; the impurity of the ears is *karṇamala*.
Urine is *mūtra* or *prasrāva*; excrement is *uccāra*, *avaskara*, *śamala*, or *śakṛt*.
*Purīṣa*, *gūtha*, *varcas*, and *viṣṭhā*—the latter two being feminine—are synonyms for feces. *Viś* is also feminine.

(2.5.666) *Karpara* and *kapāla* are masculine and neuter; *kīkasa*, *kulya*, and *asthi* also mean bone. (2.5.667) *Kaṅkāla* refers to the skeleton of the body; *kaśerukā* refers to the vertebrae of the spine. (2.5.668) *Karoṭi* (feminine) refers to the skull; *parśukā* refers to the ribs.
(2.5.669) *Aṅga*, *pratīka*, *avayava*, *apaghana*, and then *kalevara*;
(2.5.670) *gātra*, *vapuḥ*, *saṃhanana*, *śarīra*, *varṣma*, *vigraha*;
(2.5.671) *kāya*, *deha*—these are masculine and neuter; while *mūrti*, *tanu*, and *tanūḥ* are feminine.
(2.5.672) *Pādāgra* and *prapada* denote the tip of the foot; *pāda*, *pada*, *aṅghri*, and *caraṇa* denote the foot and are not feminine.
(2.5.673) The two knots at that [foot] are the *ghuṭika* and *gulpha* (the ankle); the *pārṣṇi* is the part below those two.
(2.5.674) The *jaṅghā* is the extended lower leg; *jānu*, *ūru-parva*, and *aṣṭhīvat* denote the knee and are not feminine.

(2.5.675) *Sakthi* is neuter; *ūru* is masculine; the joint of that [leg] is *vaṅkṣaṇa*, which is masculine. (2.5.676) *Guda*, *apāna*, and *pāyu* denote the anus; *basti* is the part below the navel, used in both genders. (2.5.677) *Kaṭa* is masculine; *kaṭi*, *śroṇi*, and *kakudmatī* denote the hip-bone or the pelvic region.
(2.5.678) The part behind the hips of a woman is called *nitamba*; however, the front part is *jaghana* (a neuter noun).

(2.5.679) The two depressions situated on the *nitamba* are *kakundara*, used in both genders. (2.5.680) The two fleshy parts of the buttocks are *sphic* (feminine); *kaṭiprotha* is another term for them. *Upastha* refers to the two organs about to be described.
(2.5.681) *Bhaga* and *yoni* are two terms for the female organ; *śiśna*, *meḍhra*, *mehana*, and *śephas* are [synonyms] for the penis.
(2.5.682) *Muṣka*, *aṇḍakośa*, and *vṛṣaṇa* refer to the scrotum; the region below the spinal column is called *trika*.
(2.5.683) *Picaṇḍa*, *kukṣi*, *jaṭhara*, *udara*, and *tunda* denote the belly; *stana* and *kuca* denote the breasts.

(2.5.684) *Cūcuka* is the tip of the breast; it is not masculine. *Kroḍa* is the space between the arms. (2.5.685) *Uras*, *vatsa*, and *vakṣas* denote the chest. *Pṛṣṭha* is the hind part of the body.
(2.5.686) *Skandha*, *bhujaśiras*, and *aṃsa* denote the shoulder; *jatru* refers to the two joints of that very [shoulder].
(2.5.687) Both *kakṣa* refer to the armpits; the region below them is *pārśva*, which is not feminine.

(2.5.688) *Madhyama*, *avalagna*, and *madhya* denote the waist; *madhya* is not feminine. The other two [terms] apply to both genders. (2.5.689) *Bhuja*, *bāhu*, and *praveṣṭa* denote the arm; *doḥ* is also used for it. *Kaphoṇi* and *kūrpara* denote the elbow.
Above this [the forearm], there should be the *pragaṇḍa*, and below that is the *prakoṣṭha*.
From the *maṇibandha* to the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*), the outer part of the hand is the *karabha*.
The hand has five branches; it is called *śaya*, *pāṇi*, or *hasta*. The *tarjanī* is the *pradeśinī*.

(2.5.693) The fingers are the branches of the hand; among them, the thumb is *aṅguṣṭhaḥ* (masculine), and [the others are] the forefinger (*pradeśinī*), (2.5.694) the middle finger (*madhyamā*), the ring finger (*anāmikā*), and the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*) respectively.
(2.5.695) Furthermore, *punarbhavaḥ*, *kararuhaḥ*, *nakhaḥ* (not feminine), and *nakharaḥ* (not feminine) denote the nail.
(2.5.696) When extended with the index finger and the others, [the hand] is called a *prādeśa*, a *tāla*, or a *gokarṇa*.
(2.5.697) With the thumb and the little finger extended, it is a *vitasti*, measuring twelve *aṅgulas*.
(2.5.698) When the fingers are spread out in the hand, they are called *capeṭa*, *pratala*, or *prahasta*.

(2.5.699) The two hands joined together, with their palms and surfaces pressed flat, whether left or right; (2.5.700) a hand with the fingers bent inward is a *prasṛti*; those two [hands] joined together form the masculine *añjali*.
(2.5.701) A *hasta* is a forearm with the hand extended; however, when the fist is clenched...
(2.5.702) That [measure] is a *ratni*; an *aratni*, however, is [the span] of a fist with the little finger extended.
(2.5.703) A *vyāma* is the distance between the two outstretched arms when they are extended horizontally from each other.
(2.5.704) When measuring the height of a man with his arms and hands raised, it is called *pauruṣa* in the three genders.
(2.5.705) *kaṇṭha* and *gala* are the throat; furthermore, *śirodhi* and *kandharā* also refer to the neck.
(2.5.706) A neck with three lines is called *kambugrīvā*; *avaṭu*, *ghāṭā*, and *kṛkāṭikā* refer to the nape of the neck.
(2.5.707) *Vaktra*, *āsya*, *vadana*, *tuṇḍa*, *ānana*, *lapana*, and *mukha* are synonyms for the face or mouth.
(2.5.708) For the nose, the neuter forms are *ghrāṇam*, *gandhavahā*, *ghoṇā*, *nāsā*, and *nāsikā*.
(2.5.709) The lips are *oṣṭha* and *adhara*, also called *radanacchadau* and *daśanavāsasī*.
(2.5.710) Below that is the chin (*cibukam*); the cheeks are *gaṇḍau* and *kapolau*; and the jaw below that is *hanuḥ*.
(2.5.711) *radanā*, *daśanā*, *dantāḥ*, and *radāḥ* are synonyms for teeth; *tālu* and *kākuda* refer to the palate.
(2.5.712) *rasajñā*, *rasanā*, and *jihvā* are synonyms for the tongue; *sṛkkiṇī* refers to the two corners of the lips.
(2.5.713) *lalāṭa* and *alikam* refer to the forehead; *godhi* refers to the area above the eyes; and *bhruvau* (in the feminine) refers to the two eyebrows.
(2.5.714) *Kūrca* is not feminine; it refers to the space between the eyebrows. *Tārakā* is the pupil of the eye.

(2.5.715) *Locana*, *nayana*, *netra*, *īkṣaṇa*, *cakṣus*, and *akṣi* are synonyms for the eye. (2.5.716) *Dṛk* and *dṛṣṭi* also denote the eye. *Aśru*, *netrāmbu*, *rodana*, *aśru*, and *aśru* refer to tears.
(2.5.717) *Apāṅgau* are the two outer corners of the eyes; *kaṭākṣa* is a sidelong glance.
(2.5.718) *Karṇa*, *śabdagraha*, *śrotra*, *śruti* (feminine), *śravaṇa*, and *śrava* denote the ear.
(2.5.719) *Uttamāṅga*, *śiras*, *śīrṣa*, *mūrdhan*, and *mastaka* (not feminine) denote the head.

(2.5.720) *Cikura*, *kuntala*, *bāla*, *kaca*, *keśa*, and *śiroruha* are synonyms for hair. (2.5.721) The mass of that [hair] is called *kaiśika* or *kaiśya*; *alakāḥ* refers to curled locks of hair.
(2.5.722) When these are on the forehead, they are called *bhramarakāḥ*; *kākapakṣaḥ* and *śikhaṇḍakaḥ* refer to the tuft of hair at the back of the head.

(2.5.723) *Kabara* is a style of hair arrangement; *dhammilla* refers to hair tied up. (2.5.724) *Śikhā*, *cūḍā*, and *keśapāśī* denote a tuft of hair; for one under a religious vow (*vratin*), however, these are called *saṭā* or *jaṭā*.
(2.5.725) *Veṇī* and *praveṇī* refer to braided hair; *śīrṣaṇya* and *śirasya* refer to hair on the head that is clean or well-groomed.
(2.5.726) *Pāśa*, *pakṣa*, and *hasta* follow the word *kaca* when they mean a "collection" (*kalāpa*).
(2.5.727) *Tanūruha*, *roma*, and *loma* denote body hair; the growth of that on the face of a man is called *śmaśru*.
(2.5.728) *Ākalpa*, *veṣa*, *nepathya*, *pratikarma*, and *prasādhana* denote dress and adornment.
(2.5.729) These ten [terms] apply to three genders: *alaṃkartṛ*, *alaṃkariṣṇu*, and *maṇḍita*;
(2.5.730) *prasādhita*, *alaṃkṛta*, *bhūṣita*, and *pariṣkṛta*;
(2.5.731) *vibhrāj*, *bhrājiṣṇu*, and *rociṣṇu*. *Bhūṣaṇa* shall be the ornament, and *alaṃkriyā* the act of adorning.

(2.5.732) *Alaṅkāra*, *ābharaṇa*, *pariṣkāra*, and *vibhūṣaṇa* denote ornaments; (2.5.733) so too does *maṇḍana*. Furthermore, *mukuṭa* and *kirīṭa* (which may be masculine or neuter) refer to a crown; (2.5.734) *cūdāmaṇi* and *śiroratna* refer to a crest-jewel, while *tarala* refers to the central gem of a necklace.

(2.5.735) *vālapāśyā*, *pāritathyā*, *patrapāśyā*, and *lalāṭikā* [are ornaments for the hair or forehead]; (2.5.736) *karṇikā*, *tālapatram*, and *karṇaveṣṭanam* refer to an earring; (2.5.737) *graiveyakam* is an ornament for the neck, while *lambanam* and *lalantikā* denote a long necklace or pendant.
(2.5.738) A *prālambikā* is made of gold, while an *uraḥsūtrikā* is made of pearls.

(2.5.739) A *hāra* is a string of pearls; that which consists of one hundred strings is called *devacchanda*. (2.5.740) Varieties of necklaces arise from the difference in the number of strings, such as the *guccha*, *gucchārdha*, and *gostana*.
(2.5.741) An *ardhahāra* is a necklace for a young boy; an *ekāvalī* consists of a single string.

(2.5.742) That same [necklace], when made of twenty-seven pearls, is called a *nakṣatramālā*. (2.5.743) An *āvāpaka*, *pārihārya*, *kaṭaka*, and *valaya* are terms for a bracelet; they are not feminine.
(2.5.744) Keyūra and aṅgada are synonyms; aṅgulīyaka and ūrmikā [are synonyms].
(2.5.745) Aṅgulimudrā with letters inscribed upon it is called sākṣarā; kaṅkaṇa is an ornament for the hand.
(2.5.746) On a woman's waist, mekhalā, kāñcī, saptakī, and likewise raśanā [denote the girdle].
(2.5.747) *Sārasana* is neuter; furthermore, *śṛṅkhala* (a chain) is used for the male hip and is of three genders.
(2.5.748) *Pādāṅgada*, *tulākoṭi*, *mañjīra*, and *nūpura* (anklet) are not feminine.
(2.5.749) *Haṃsaka* is an anklet, *pādakaṭaka* is a foot-ring, and *kiṅkiṇī* is a small bell.
(2.5.750) Bark, wood, insects, and wool—these ten are the sources of cloth in the three genders.

(2.5.751–752) Cloth made from bark is *vālka*; that from flax and the like is *kṣauma*; that from cotton is *phāla*, as is that from *bādara* (hemp); that arising from the cocoon of an insect is *kauśeya*; and that produced from the hair of a deer is *rāṅkava*.
(2.5.753) *Anāhata*, *niṣpravāṇi*, and *tantraka* refer to new garments.
(2.5.754) *Udgrathanīya* refers to a pair of washed garments.
(2.5.755) *Patrorṇa* is washed silk; it is highly valuable and very costly.
(2.5.756) *Kṣauma* and *dukūla* refer to linen cloth; the two terms *nivīta* and *prāvṛta* apply to three genders.
(2.5.757) In the feminine plural, they denote the fringes (*daśā*) of a garment; *vastra* refers to both [the garment and its parts].
(2.5.758) *Dairghya*, *āyāma*, and *āroha* mean length; *pariṇāha* and *viśālatā* mean breadth.
(2.5.759) *paṭaccara* means a worn-out garment; *naktaka* and *karpaṭa* are synonyms.
(2.5.760) *Vastra*, *ācchādana*, *vāsa*, *cela*, *vasana*, and *aṃśuka* all mean clothing.
(2.5.761) *Sucelaka* and *paṭa* (the latter not feminine) refer to fine cloth; *varāśi* and *sthūlaśāṭaka* denote a coarse or thick garment.
(2.5.762) *Nicola* and *pracchadapaṭa* are synonyms; *rallaka* and *kambala* are also synonymous.
(2.5.763) *Antarīya*, *upasaṃvyāna*, and *paridhāna* refer to the lower garment.
(2.5.764) *Prāvāra* and *uttarāsaṅga* are synonymous; likewise, *bṛhatikā* is the same.
(2.5.765) *Saṃvyāna* and *uttarīya* mean an upper garment; *cola* and *kūrpāsaka* refer to a bodice, not feminine.
(2.5.766) *Nīśāra* refers to a cloak used for warding off cold winds.
(2.5.767) *Ardhoruka* is the short tunic of excellent women; *śaṇḍātaka* is a loincloth, not feminine.
(2.5.768) That which reaches as far as the forepart of the feet is *āprapadīna*; it is used in three genders.
(2.5.769) *Vitāna*, *ulloca*, and *dūṣya* refer to a canopy or awning, such as a cloth covering for a tent.
(2.5.770) *Pratisīrā*, *javanikā*, and *tiraskariṇī* denote a curtain or screen.
(2.5.771) *Parikarma* is the refinement of the limbs; *mārṣṭi*, *mārjanā*, and *mṛjā* mean cleansing.
(2.5.772) *Udvartana* and *utsādana* are two synonymous terms for rubbing with unguents; *āplāva* and *āplava* mean immersion.
(2.5.773) *Snāna* means bathing; *carcā*, *cārcikya*, and *sthāsaka* refer to anointing with fragrant substances, while *prabodhana* refers to awakening [the senses].
(2.5.774) *anubodhaḥ* and *patralekhā* [are synonyms for a decorative mark]; *patrāṅguli*—these two are identical.
(2.5.775) A forehead mark made with *tamāla* leaves, or with *tilaka* or *citraka* [pigments], is called a *viśeṣaka*.
(2.5.776) The second and fourth [of these terms] do not apply to a woman; furthermore, [the term *viśeṣaka* does not apply to] saffron (*kuṅkuma*).
(2.5.777) That which is born in Kāśmīra is called agniśikha; it is excellent when yellowed by the Bāhlīka country.
(2.5.778) It is known as lohitacandana, which indicates the contraction of blood and is steadfast.
(2.5.779) Lākṣā, rākṣā, and jatu are neuter; yāva, alakta, and drumāmaya are synonyms for lac.
(2.5.780) *lavaṅga*, *devakusuma*, and *śrīsaṃjña* are synonyms for cloves; then *jāyaka*.
(2.5.781) *Kālīyaka*, *kālānusārya*, and *samārthaka* are synonyms for black sandalwood.
(2.5.782) *Vaṃśika*, *aguru*, *rājārha*, *lohakṛmija*, and *joṅgaka* are synonyms for aloe-wood (*aguru*).
(2.5.783) *Kālāguru* and *aguru* are types of aloe-wood; that which has the fragrance of jasmine (*malli*) is called *maṅgalyā*.
(2.5.784) *Yakṣadhūpa*, *sarjarasa*, *rāla*, and *sarvarasa* are synonyms for resin. (2.5.785) *Bahurūpa* is also [a type of resin]; furthermore, there are *vṛkadhūpa* and *kṛtrimadhūpa*.
(2.5.786) Turuṣka, piṇḍaka, sihlaka, and also yāvana; then pāyasa, (2.5.787) śrīvāsa, vṛkadhūpa, as well as śrīveṣṭa and saraladrava; (2.5.788) mṛganābhi, mṛgamada, and kastūrī; and then kolaka.
Kaṅkolaka and kośaphala are synonyms; furthermore, karpūra is not feminine.
Tailaparṇika and gośīrṣa are synonyms for haricandana, which is not feminine.
Tilaparṇī, however, refers to patrāṅga, rañjana, and raktacandana.
(2.5.792) *Kucandana* is [a type of sandalwood]; furthermore, *jātīkośa* and *jātīphala* are synonyms.
(2.5.793) *Yakṣakardama* consists of camphor, agallochum, musk, and *kakkola*.
(2.5.794) *Gātrānulepanī*, *varti*, *varṇaka*, and *vilepana* refer to unguents for the body.
(2.5.795) Powders used for perfuming are called *vāsa-yogāḥ*; that which has been infused with fragrance is termed *bhāvita* or *vāsita*, used in three genders.
(2.5.796) The refinement (*saṃskāra*) effected by means of perfumes, garlands, and the like is known as *adhivāsana*.
(2.5.797) A garland worn on the head is called *mālya*, *mālā*, or *sraj*; one worn amidst the hair is called *garbhaka*.

(2.5.798) That which hangs from the crest-lock is *prabhraṣṭaka*; that placed in front is *lalāmaka*. (2.5.799) A *prālamba* hangs straight down from the neck; however, when it is cast diagonally across the chest, it is called *vaikakṣika*. *Āpīḍa* and *śekhara* refer to ornaments worn upon the crest-locks.
(2.5.801) *Racanā* means arrangement, spreading out, expansion, or fullness.
(2.5.802) *Upadhāna* and *upabarha* refer to a pillow; they are synonymous with *śayanīya* when referring to bedding.
(2.5.803) *Śayana*, *mañca*, *paryaṅka*, *palyaṅka*, and *khaṭvā* are synonymous terms for a bed or couch.

(2.5.804) *genduka* is a ball; *kanduka* is a ball; *dīpa* is a lamp; *pradīpa* is a lamp; *pīṭha* is a seat. (2.5.805) *samudgaka* is a casket; *saṃpuṭaka* is a casket; *pratigrāha* is a spittoon; *patadgraha* is a spittoon. (2.5.806) *prasādhanī* is a comb; *kaṅkatikā* is a comb; *piṣṭāta* is a scented powder; *paṭavāsaka* is a scented powder.
(2.5.807) *Darpaṇa*, *mukura*, and *ādarśa* mean mirror; *vyajana* and *tālavṛntaka* mean a fan.
Thus ends the section on humans (2.6.808).
