*Saṃtati*, *gotra*, *janana*, *kula*, *abhijana*, and *anvaya* mean lineage or family.

Now, the section on the Brahmins (2.6.809): *vaṃśa*, *anvavāya*, and *saṃtāna* denote lineage. *Varṇas* are the [social classes] beginning with the Brāhmaṇas (2.6.810): the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra; these are known as the fourfold caste system (*cāturvarṇya*).
(2.6.811) One born of royal seed is *rājabījī*, and one belonging to the royal lineage is *rājavaṃśya*; however, one born of a noble family is *bījya*.
(2.6.812) *Mahākula*, *kulīna*, *ārya*, *sabhya*, *sajjana*, and *sādhu* all denote those of high birth or virtuous character.
(2.6.813) The four stages of life consist of the student (*brahmacārī*), the householder (*gṛhī*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the mendicant (*bhikṣu*).
(2.6.814) *Āśrama* is not feminine; *dvijāti*, *agrajanman*, *bhūdeva*, and *vāḍava* are synonyms for a Brahmin.
(2.6.815) He is also called *vipra* and *brāhmaṇa*; he is one whose six duties (*ṣaṭkarmā*) consist of performing sacrifices and other such rites.
(2.6.816) *Vidvān*, *vipaścit*, *doṣajña*, *satsudhī*, *kovida*, and *budha* denote a learned man.
(2.6.817) Dhīraḥ, manīṣī, jñaḥ, prājñaḥ, saṃkhyāvān, paṇḍitaḥ, kaviḥ;
(2.6.818) dhīmān, sūriḥ, kṛtī, kṛṣṭiḥ, labdhavarṇaḥ, vicakṣaṇaḥ;
(2.6.819) dūradarśī, dīrghadarśī; śrotriya and chāndasa are synonyms.
A Mīmāṃsaka is one who follows Jaimini; a Vedāntin is one who adheres to the doctrine of Brahman. One who follows the Vaiśeṣika system is an Aulūkya; a follower of the Śūnyavāda is a Saugata.
A Naiyāyika is an Akṣapāda; an advocate of Syādvāda is an Ārhaka.
(2.6.823) The Cārvāka and the Lokāyatika; the Sāṃkhya and the Kāpila [believe] in the pre-existence of the effect (satkārya).
(2.6.824) An *upādhyāya* is a teacher (*adhyāpaka*); furthermore, one who performs the *niṣeka* and other rites is a *guru*.
(2.6.825) One who explains the mantras is an *ācārya*; however, one who prescribes vows in a sacrifice (*adhvara*) is a *vratī*.
(2.6.826) He who has sacrificed and he who is sacrificing is one consecrated for the Soma sacrifice.
(2.6.827) One whose nature is to sacrifice is a *yāyajūka*; one who has sacrificed according to the rules is a *yajvan*.
(2.6.828) By means of the *gīrpati* sacrifice, he becomes a *sthapati*; one who drinks the Soma is a *somapīthin*, while a *somapa* is simply a drinker of Soma.
(2.6.829) He by whom a sacrifice has been performed in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee has [the merit of] all the Vedas.

(2.6.830) An *anūcāna* is one who has studied the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*) from a teacher. (2.6.831) One who has received permission [to leave] is a *samāvṛtta*; but one who has performed the consecration ceremony is a *sutvā*.

(2.6.832) *Chātra* and *antevāsin* refer to a disciple; *śaikṣas* are those who are beginners. (2.6.833) Those who share the same Veda, vows, and conduct are *sabrahmacārin*s toward one another. (2.6.834) However, those who have the same teacher are *satīrthya*s; one who has piled the fire-altar is an *agnicit*.
(2.6.835) *Aitihya* is that which consists of traditional instruction; *itihā* is an indeclinable [used in the same sense].
(2.6.836) *Upajñā* is the first knowledge; *upakrama* is the undertaking after having gained knowledge.
(2.6.837) *Yajña*, *sava*, *adhvara*, *yāga*, *saptatantu*, *makha*, and *kratu* are synonyms for sacrifice.
(2.6.838) Recitation, fire-offerings, honoring guests, libations, and the bali offering—
(2.6.839) these are the five great sacrifices, known by names such as the Brahma-sacrifice and others.
(2.6.840) *Samajyā*, *pariṣad*, *goṣṭhī*, *sabhā*, *samiti*, and *saṃsad* [are synonyms for an assembly].
(2.6.841) *Āsthānī* is neuter, while *āsthānam* is both feminine and neuter; *sadaḥ* [is also used for an assembly].

(2.6.842) The *prāgvaṃśa* is the area before the sacrificial hall (*havirgeha*). (2.6.843) Those who perceive the ritual rules are called *sadasyas*; they are also known as *sabhāsadas*, *sabhāstārās*, *sabhyās*, and *sāmājikās*.
(2.6.844) The Adhvaryu, Udgātṛ, and Hotṛ are, respectively, those who know the Yajus, Sāman, and Ṛc.
(2.6.845) The Āgnīdhra and others are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and sacrificers (*yājaka*), who are to be chosen for their wealth.
(2.6.846) The *vedi* is a consecrated ground; it is a leveled area known as a *sthaṇḍila* or *catvara*.

(2.6.847) *Caṣāla* is the ring at the top of a sacrificial post (*yūpa*); *kumbā* is a very dense enclosure. (2.6.848) *Tarma* is the tip of the sacrificial post; *araṇi* (in both genders) refers to the wood used for kindling by friction. (2.6.849) The three fires are the *dakṣiṇāgni*, the *gārhapatya*, and the *āhavanīya*.

(2.6.850) This triad of fires is called *tretā*; *praṇīta* is the consecrated fire. (2.6.851) *Samūhya*, *paricāyya*, and *upacāyya* are technical terms applied to specific fires. (2.6.852) That which is brought forth from the *gārhapatya* fire and established as the *dakṣiṇāgni* is [the *praṇīta*].
(2.6.853) In that [context], *ānāyya* refers to the sacrificial fire; furthermore, *agnāyī* and *svāhā* are the beloveds of the consumer of oblations (*hutabhuj*).
(2.6.854) That which is used for kindling the fire is called an *ṛk*, a *sāmidhenī*, or a *dhāyyā*.
(2.6.855) The *chandas* (meter), beginning with the *gāyatrī*, is so named; and in the cooking of the oblation, the term *caru* is masculine.

(2.6.856) Āmikṣā is that which results from adding curd to milk that has been heated and cooled. (2.6.857) A *dhavitram* is a fan made of deer skin. (2.6.858) *Pṛṣadājyam* is clarified butter mixed with curd; *paramānnam*, however, is rice cooked in milk (*pāyasa*).
(2.6.859) *Havya* and *kavya* refer to food offerings for the gods and ancestors; the vessels used for these include the *sruva* and others.
(2.6.860) The *dhruvā*, *upabhṛt*, and *juhū* are names [for specific ladles], while the *sruva* is distinct; these types of *sruc* are feminine.
(2.6.861) That animal which, having been consecrated with mantras, is slain in a sacrifice is called *upākṛta*.
(2.6.862) *Śamana* and *prokṣaṇa* refer to the act of killing by means of a succession [of blows].
(2.6.863) The words *pramīta*, *upasaṃpanna*, and *prokṣita* are used for one who has been killed, and they take the gender of the noun they qualify (*vācyaliṅga*).

(2.6.864) *Sāṃnāyya* refers to the sacrificial oblation; that which is offered into the fire is called *huta*, and it is used in the three genders when referring to what is consecrated with the exclamation *vaṣaṭ*.
(2.6.865) *Avabhṛtha* is the concluding bath at the end of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) in a sacrifice; that which is fit for such ritual action is called *yajñiya*.

(2.6.866) Furthermore, among the three types of meritorious acts, those performed during a sacrificial rite (*kratu*) are termed *iṣṭa*, while works such as digging wells and so forth are termed *pūrta*.
(2.6.867) *Amṛta* refers to the remains of a sacrifice (*vighasa*), specifically the remnants of the sacrificial food and the remnants of the meal.
Tyāga, vihāpita, dāna, utsarjana, visarjana,
viśrāṇana, vitaraṇa, sparśana, pratipādana,
prādeśana, nirvapaṇa, apavarjana, and aṃhati are synonyms for giving.

(2.6.871) A gift made on the day of death for the sake of the deceased constitutes the three types of *aurdhvadehika* rites. (2.6.872) *Pitṛdāna* is the offering to the ancestors; *nivāpa* is the scattering [of grain]; and *śrāddha* is that specific ritual. (2.6.873) The monthly rite is called *anvāhārya*; the eighth part of the day is the *kutapa*, which is not feminine.

(2.6.874) *Paryeṣaṇā*, *parīṣṭi*, *anveṣaṇā*, and *gaveṣaṇā* mean searching. (2.6.875) *Sani* is the same as *adhyeṣaṇā*, while *yāñcā*, *abhiśasti*, *yācanā*, and *arthanā* mean begging. (2.6.876) The six [terms] beginning with *arghya* are used in three genders; *arghya* refers to that which is for the sake of honor, while *pādya* refers to water for the feet.

(2.6.877) In sequence, *ātithya* and *ātitheya* refer to that which is suitable for a guest (*atithi*). (2.6.878) *Āveśika*, *āgantu*, and *atithi* are synonyms; (2.6.879) however, the term *atithi* specifically applies to one who has arrived at a house.
*Prāghūrṇika* and *prāghūṇaka* also denote a visitor. Furthermore, *abhyutthāna* refers to the act of rising [to show respect], that is, showing honor.

(2.6.880) Worship (*pūjā*), salutation (*namasyā*), honor (*apaciti*), veneration (*saparyā*), adoration (*arcā*), and offering (*arhaṇā*) are synonyms. (2.6.881) Service (*varivasyā*), however, is attendance (*śuśrūṣā*); it is also called attendance (*paricaryā*) and waiting upon (*upāsanā*). (2.6.882) Wandering (*vrajyā*), roaming (*aṭāṭyā*), and traveling about (*paryaṭana*) are synonyms; while abiding on the path of heroes (*īryāpatha*) is termed conduct (*caryā*).

(2.6.883) Upasparśa, however, is rinsing the mouth; furthermore, mauna is non-speaking. (2.6.884) He is Prācetasa and the first poet (Ādikavi); he is also Maitrāvaruṇi. (2.6.885) He is Vālmīki, as well as Gādheya, Viśvāmitra, and Kauśika.
Vyāsa is Dvaipāyana, Pārāśarya, and the son of Satyavatī. Sequence in the feminine is vāvṛt, paripāṭhī, and anukrama.
Synonym is paryāya; while atipāta, paryaya, and upātyaya denote passing by or transgression.

(2.6.889) *Niyama* is a religious observance (*vrata*), not feminine; it consists of meritorious acts such as fasting and the like. (2.6.890) *Aupavasta* and *upavāsa* both mean fasting. (2.6.891) *Viveka* is the state of being distinct or self-separation.
*Brahmavarcasa* is excellence in conduct and Vedic study. Furthermore, *añjali* is the gesture of joining the palms.
(2.6.892) In the sacred texts, *brahmāñjali* refers to the hollowed palms joined in reverence; in the sacred texts, *vipruṣaḥ* refers to droplets, and *brahmabindavaḥ* likewise.
(2.6.893) *Brahmāsana* refers to the seat for meditation and yoga; *kalpa* and *vidhikrama* refer to ritual procedures.
(2.6.894) The primary rule is the first *kalpa*; the secondary (*anukalpa*) is inferior to that.
(2.6.895) The formal reception (*upākaraṇa*) of the Veda should be preceded by preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*), according to the sacred tradition (*śruti*).
(2.6.896) But when [the ground] is level, both the grasping of the feet and the salutation (*abhivādana*) [are performed].
(2.6.897) A mendicant (*bhikṣu*), a wandering ascetic (*parivrāj*), a follower of Karmanda (*karmandin*), a follower of Pārāśarya (*pārāśarin*), and a bearer of the staff (*maskarin*) [are synonyms].
(2.6.898) An ascetic is a *tāpasa*, a *pārikāṅkṣin*, one who restrains his speech (*vācaṃyama*), or a sage (*muni*).
(2.6.899) One who endures the hardships of austerity is self-controlled (*dānta*); those belonging to the [first] caste are students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*).
(2.6.900) Sages (*ṛṣi*) are those whose speech is truth; a graduate (*snātaka*) is one who has performed the ritual bath and observes his vows (*vratī*).
(2.6.901) Those who have conquered the collection of their senses are *yatins* and *yatayas*.

(2.6.902) He who sleeps on the bare ground by virtue of his vow is a *sthaṇḍilaśāyin*. (2.6.903) He is also called a *sthāṇḍila*; furthermore, those who have transcended the two [qualities] are *virajas* and *tamasas*.
(2.6.904) *pavitraḥ*, *prayataḥ*, and *pūtaḥ* mean pure; *pāṣaṇḍāḥ* refers to those who wear all kinds of sectarian marks.
(2.6.905) A staff made of *pālāśa* wood is called *āṣāḍha*; for a vow (*vrata*), one made of *rāmbha* (bamboo) is called *vaiṇava*.
(2.6.906) *Kamaṇḍaluḥ* and *kuṇḍī* are not feminine [and denote] the water-pot of those observing vows; *bṛṣī* is the seat of those observing vows.
(2.6.907) *Ajina* is the skin; *kṛtti* is feminine; *bhaikṣa* is a collection of alms.
(2.6.908) *Svādhyāya* is *japa* (muttering prayers); *sutyā*, *abhiṣava*, and *savana* are synonyms for the extraction of soma juice.
(2.6.909) The *aghamarṣaṇa* [hymn] is used for muttering (*japya*) to destroy all sins; it is of three types.
(2.6.910) The Darśa and Paurṇamāsa sacrifices are performed separately at the ends of the two fortnights. (2.6.911) That obligatory action which depends upon bodily means is *yama*.
(2.6.912) But *niyama* is that obligatory action which has adventitious means.
(2.6.913) *Kṣaura*, however, is the act of making auspicious; it is called *muṇḍana* and *vapana*, and these three terms apply to all genders.
(2.6.914) *Kakṣāpaṭī*, *kaupīna*, and *śāṭī* are observed to be feminine.
(2.6.915) *Upavīta* and *brahmasūtra* refer to the sacred thread when it is suspended over the right arm.
(2.6.916) When worn over the right shoulder, it is *prācīnāvīta*; when hanging from the neck, it is *nivīta*.
(2.6.917–918) The *tīrtha* for the gods (*daiva*) is at the tips of the fingers; that for humans (*kāya*) is at the base of the little finger;
that for the ancestors (*pitrya*) is between the thumb and the forefinger; and that for Brahman (*brāhma*) is at the base of the thumb.
(2.6.919) There may be *brahmabhūya*, which is the state of being Brahman (*brahmatva*), as well as union with Brahman (*brahmasāyujya*).
(2.6.920) Likewise, there is the state of being a god (*devabhūya*) and so forth; and [there is] the desired [result] from the *sāntapana* and other penances.
(2.6.921) A man who practices renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and fasting generally [attains this], whereas one who slays a hero (*vīrahā*) [falls].
One who has lost the sacred fires; one who practices hypocrisy out of greed by falsely assuming the appearance of proper conduct;

a *vrātya*, who is devoid of sacramental rites; one who neglects Vedic study; one who is excluded from the community; one who makes a public display of righteousness; one who lives merely for the sake of outward signs; one who has broken his vow of chastity; and one who has failed in his religious observances.
(2.6.925) When [the sun] sets while he is asleep, and when it rises while he is asleep,
(2.6.926) the sun is designated as *abhinirmukta* and *abhyudita* respectively;
(2.6.927) a younger brother who takes a wife while his elder brother remains unmarried is called a *parivettṛ*.

(2.6.928) But the *parivitti* is he whose younger brother marries first; the terms *vivāha*, *upayama*, (2.6.929) as well as *pariṇaya*, *udvāha*, *upayāma*, and *pāṇipīḍana* are synonyms for marriage.
(2.6.930) *Vyavāya*, *grāmyadharma*, *maithuna*, *nidhuvana*, and *rata* denote sexual intercourse.
(2.6.931) The *trivarga* consists of virtue (*dharma*), pleasure (*kāma*), and wealth (*artha*); with liberation (*mokṣa*) added, it becomes the *caturvarga*.
(2.6.932) When these four are accompanied by strength (*bala*), they constitute the *caturbhadra*. Those who are well-disposed toward the bridegroom are called *janyas*.
Thus ends the section on the Brahmins (*brahmavarga*).
(2.7.933) Anointed at the head (*mūrdhābhiṣikta*), a member of the royal caste (*rājanya*), born of the arms (*bāhuja*), a Kṣatriya, and a sovereign (*virāṭ*).
Now begins the section on Kṣatriyas (2.7.934):

A king (*rājā*), a ruler (*rāṭ*), one who supports the earth (*pārthiva*), a sustainer of the ground (*kṣmābhṛt*), a leader of men (*nṛpa*), a protector of the land (*bhūpa*), and a lord of the earth (*mahīkṣit*).
(2.7.935) But a king over whom all the vassal lords have bowed is a sovereign lord (*adhīśvara*).
(2.7.936) A universal monarch (*cakravartin*) is a ruler of the whole earth (*sārvabhauma*); any other king is a lord of a province (*maṇḍaleśvara*).
(2.7.937) He by whom the *rājasūya* sacrifice has been performed, and who is the lord of a circle of kings (*maṇḍala*), [is a universal monarch].

He who rules by the command of a king is a *samrāj* (emperor); then, the collective body of kings is called *rājakam* or *rājanyakam*, respectively, when referring to a group of monarchs or *kṣatriyas*.
A minister is a *mantrī*, *dhīsaciva*, or *amātya*; others are *karmasacivas* (executive ministers).

(2.7.941) *Mahāmātra* refers to chief ministers; *purodhāḥ* and *purohitaḥ* refer to the domestic priest. (2.7.942) *Prāḍvivākaḥ*, *akṣadarśakaḥ*, and *draṣṭā* refer to one who examines legal disputes. (2.7.943) *Pratīhāraḥ*, *dvārapālaḥ*, *dvāsthaḥ*, *dvāsthitaḥ*, and *darśakaḥ* refer to the doorkeeper.
The bodyguard is the *anīkastha*; furthermore, *adhyakṣa* and *adhikṛta* are synonyms.
A *sthāyuka* is an official appointed over a single village, while a *gopa* oversees many villages.
The superintendent of gold is the *bhaurika*, whereas the superintendent of silver is the *naiṣkika*.
(2.7.947) A person appointed over the inner apartments is called *antarvaṃśika*.
(2.7.948) They are also known as *sauvidalla*, *kañcukin*, *sthāpatya*, and *sauvida*.
(2.7.949) *Śaṇḍha* and *varṣavara* are synonymous; they are servants, dependents, and those who live under others.
(2.7.950) A king whose territory is immediately adjacent is an enemy; beyond him is a friend. (2.7.951) One further beyond is neutral; one behind is an attacker (*pārṣṇigrāha*).
(2.7.952) *Ripu*, *vairin*, *sapatna*, *ari*, *dviṣat*, *dveṣaṇa*, and *durhṛd* denote an enemy.
(2.7.953) *dviṭ*, *vipakṣa*, *ahita*, *amitra*, *dasyu*, *śātrava*, and *śatru* [mean enemy];
(2.7.954) *abhighātin*, *para*, *arāti*, *pratyarthin*, and *paripanthin* [also mean enemy];
(2.7.955) *vayasya*, *snigdha*, and *savayas* [mean a companion], while *mitra*, *sakhi*, and *suhṛd* [mean a friend].
(2.7.956) Friendship is *sāptapadīna*; compliance is *anurodha* or *anuvartana*.
(2.7.957) A spy is called *yathārhavarṇa*, *praṇidhi*, *apasarpa*, *cara*, *spaśa*, or *cāra*.
(2.7.958) A secret agent is also a *gūḍhapuruṣa*; *āpta* and *pratyayita* are synonyms for one who is trusted.
(2.7.959) A *sāṃvatsara* is an astronomer (*jyautiṣika*), as well as a knower of fate (*daivajña*) and an astrologer (*gaṇaka*).
(2.7.960) One may also be called a *mauhūrtika*, a *mauhūrta*, a *jñānika*, or a *kārtāntika*.
(2.7.961) A *tāntrika* is one who knows the established doctrines (*siddhānta*); a *satrī* and a *gṛhapati* are synonyms.
(2.7.962) *lipikāraḥ*, *akṣaracaraṇaḥ*, and *akṣaracuñcuḥ* refer to a scribe (*lekhaka*).
(2.7.963) *Lipiḥ* and *libhiḥ* refer to the arrangement of written characters (*likhitākṣaravinyāsaḥ*) or their configuration (*saṃsthāna*).

The word *irubhe* means "two women" (2.7.964). A messenger who carries a message is called a *dūta*; the state or activity of being such a messenger is *dūtya* (2.7.965). One who travels on a road is termed *adhvanīna*, *adhvaga*, *adhvanya*, *pāntha*, or *pathika*.

The sovereign, the ministers, the allies, the treasury, the realm, the fortresses, and the army—these are the constituent elements of sovereignty (*rājyāṅga*). The subjects (*prakṛti*) include the guilds of the city-dwellers as well. Furthermore, there are peace, war, marching, halting, dividing the army, and seeking refuge.
(2.7.969) The six measures of policy (*ṣaḍguṇāḥ*); the three powers (*śaktayaḥ*) arising from majesty, energy, and counsel;
(2.7.970) decline, stability, and growth—the triad that constitutes the goal for those who know statecraft (*nītivedinām*);
(2.7.971) that which is born of the treasury and the army is majesty (*pratāpaḥ*), power (*prabhāvaḥ*), and splendor (*tejaḥ*).

(2.7.972) Division, punishment, conciliation, and bribery—these are the fourfold set of expedients. (2.7.973) Violence and punishment are synonyms; likewise, conciliation and gentleness are synonymous.
(2.7.974) *Upadhā* is the testing of [an official] by means of [temptations involving] dharma and so forth, through the instigation of dissension.
(2.7.975) Among the three [types of spies], there are five; that which is not shared (*aṣaḍakṣīṇa*) is that which is beyond the range of the third [person] and those following.
(2.7.976) *Vivikta*, *vijana*, *channa*, *niḥśalāka*, and likewise *rahaḥ* [are synonyms for a secluded place].
*Rahas* and *upāṃśu* mean "in secret" when not used as technical grammatical terms; that which pertains to them is called *rahasya*, used in three genders.
*Visrambha* and *viśvāsa* are synonyms meaning "confidence. *Bhreṣa* and *bhraṃśa* mean falling away from what is appropriate.
*Abhreṣa*, *anyāyakalpa*, *deśarūpa*, and *samañjasa* mean "correct" or "proper."

(2.7.980) *yukta*, *aupayika*, *labhya*, and *bhajamāna* mean "suitable" or "fitting"; (2.7.981) *abhinīta* means "polished" or "refined," while *nyāyya* means "just" or "proper"—these six terms refer to what is appropriate; (2.7.982) *saṃpradhāraṇā* means "deliberation" or "investigation," while *samarthana* means "justification" or "supporting an argument. Furthermore, *avavāda*, *nirdeśa*, *nideśa*, and *śāsana* all signify "instruction" or "command."
(2.7.983) *Śiṣṭi* means instruction or command; *saṃsthā*, however, means a limit, a boundary, maintenance, or stability.
(2.7.984) *Sudharaṇā*, *sudhārā*, and *susthiti* are feminine [terms for a firm support]; *sudaśonnati* is [a term for] excellence.
(2.7.985) *Āgas*, *aparādhas*, and *mantus* are synonyms for an offense; *uddāna* and *bandhana* are the same [meaning a binding].
(2.7.986) A double tax on those with two-footed animals is called *bhāgadheya*, *kara*, or *bali*.
(2.7.987) What is to be given at ferries and the like is *śulka* (not feminine); *prābhṛta*, *pradeśana*, (2.7.988) *upāyana*, *upagrāhya*, *upahāra*, and likewise *upadā* [denote a gift].
(2.7.989) But that which is to be given as a dowry and so forth, that is *sudāya*; it is also called *haraṇa*.
(2.7.990) The present time is *tadātva*, while the subsequent time is *āyati*.
(2.7.991) Immediate fruit is *sāndṛṣṭika* or *sadyas*; future fruit is *udarka*.
(2.7.992) Fire, water, and so forth are "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*); that which arises from one's own or another's army is "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*).
(2.7.993) For kings, there is fear of serpents and fear arising from one's own faction.
(2.7.994) *Prakriyā* refers to administrative authority (*adhikāra*), while *cāmara* refers to a fly-whisk (*prakīrṇaka*).
(2.7.995) That which is the king’s throne is called a *bhadrāsana*, while a *siṃhāsana* is likewise; (2.7.996) a golden umbrella is an *ātapatra*, serving as the royal insignia of a king;
(2.7.997) a *bhadrakumbha* is a full water-jar, and a *bhṛṅgāra* is a golden ewer.
(2.7.998) *Niveśa* and *śibira* are neuter; *sajjana* means protection.
(2.7.999) An elephant, horse, chariot, and infantry constitute the fourfold components of an army (*senāṅga*).
(2.7.1000) *Dantī*, *dantāvala*, *hastī*, *dvirada*, *anekapa*, and *dvipa* denote an elephant.
(2.7.1001) *Mataṅgaja*, *gaja*, *nāga*, *kuñjara*, *vāraṇa*, and *karī* are synonyms for elephant.
(2.7.1002) *Ibha*, *stamberama*, and *padmī* also denote an elephant; the leader of the herd is called *yūthanātha* or *yūthapa*.
(2.7.1003) *Madotkaṭa* and *madakala* refer to one in rut, while *kalabha* is a young elephant.
(2.7.1004) *Prabhinna*, *garjita*, and *matta* are synonyms for an elephant in rut; *udvānta* and *nirmada* are equivalent terms for one whose rut has ceased.
(2.7.1005) *Hāstika* and *gajatā* refer to a herd of elephants; *kariṇī*, *dhenukā*, and *vaśā* denote a female elephant.
(2.7.1006) *Gaṇḍa*, *kaṭa*, *mada*, *dāna*, *vamathu*, and *karaśīkara* all refer to the temporal juice or ichor flowing from an elephant's temples.
The two *kumbhas* are the two fleshy protuberances of the head; the wise know that between them is the *pumān*.

The *avagraha* is the forehead (*lalāṭa*), while the *īṣikā* is the ridge of the eye (*akṣikūṭaka*). The region of the outer corner of the eye is the *niryāṇa*, and the root of the ear is the *cūlikā*.
(2.7.1010) Below the pot is the *vāhittha*; that which is below it is the *pratimāna*.
(2.7.1011) The shoulder region is the *āsana*; the *padmaka* is the network of dots. (2.7.1012) The side portion is the *pakṣabhāga*, while the portion at the front is the *dantabhāga*.
(2.7.1013) The two regions of the fore- and hind-legs are respectively called the *gātra* and the *avara*.

(2.7.1014) A goad is a *totra*, a tethering rope is an *ālāna*; furthermore, a chain used for binding at a pillar is an *anduka* or *nigaḍa* (neuter). (2.7.1015) An elephant hook is an *aṅkuśa* (not feminine), while *sṛṇi* is feminine.
(2.7.1016) *dūṣyā*, *cūṣā*, *kakṣyā*, and *varatrā* are synonyms for a leather thong; *kalpanā* and *sajjanā* are the same [meaning "harness" or "equipment"].

(2.7.1017) *praveṇī*, *āstaraṇa*, *varṇa*, *paristoma*, and *kutha* refer to an elephant rug or blanket (the latter two being used for both genders). (2.7.1018) *vīta* refers to a weak or inferior elephant or horse; *vārī* is a term for an elephant's tethering post.
(2.7.1019) *Ghoṭaka*, *vīti* (*pīti*), *turaga*, *turaṅga*, *aśva*, and *turaṅgama*; (2.7.1020) *vājin*, *vāha*, *arvan*, *gandharva*, *haya*, *saindhava*, and *sapti*.
(2.7.1021) Those that are well-bred, of noble lineage, well-trained, and excellent carriers are called *ājāneya*.
(2.7.1022) Horses from Vanāyu, Pārasīka, Kāmboja, and Bāhlīka are [distinguished by their origin].
(2.7.1023) A horse fit for the *aśvamedha* sacrifice is called *yayuraśva*, while one that is exceedingly swift is called *javana*.
(2.7.1024) *pṛṣṭhyaḥ*, *sthaurī*, *sitaḥ*, and *karkaḥ* denote a white horse; *rathyaḥ* refers to one who is a carrier of a chariot.
(2.7.1025) *bālaḥ* and *kiśoraḥ* refer to a young horse; *vāmī* and *aśvā* refer to a mare; *vāḍavaḥ* refers to a herd of horses.
(2.7.1026) *āśvīnam* is used in three genders to denote that which can be traversed by a horse in a single day.
(2.7.1027) But the neighing of middle-sized horses is called *heṣā* or *hreṣā*, as well as *nisvana*.
(2.7.1028) The region of the throat is the *nigāla*; however, a herd [of horses] is called *aśvīya* or *āśva*.
(2.7.1029) *Āskandita*, *dhauritaka*, *recita*, *valgita*, and *pluta* [are the five modes of galloping].
(2.7.1030) These five are the gaits; *ghoṇā* and *protha* denote the nose, and are used in both genders.
(2.7.1031) *Kavikā* and *khalīna* denote the bit, and are not feminine; *śapha* is neuter, while *khura* is masculine.
(2.7.1032) *Puccha*, *lūma*, and *lāṅgūla* denote the tail, and are not feminine; *vālahasta* and *vāladhi* are also used for the tail.
(2.7.1033) *Upāvṛtta* and *luṭhita* refer to a chariot that has turned back or rolled over on the ground repeatedly.

(2.7.1034) A war-chariot equipped with wheels is called a *śatāṅga*, a *syandana*, or a *ratha*. (2.7.1035) That which is not for the purpose of battle, being a wheeled vehicle for pleasure, is a *puṣparatha*.
(2.7.1036) *Karṇīratha*, *pravahaṇa*, and *ḍayana*—these three are synonymous.
(2.7.1037) *Anaḥ* and *śakaṭa* are neuter; *gantrī* is feminine and refers to a cart drawn by oxen.
(2.7.1038) *Śibikā* is a palanquin (*yāpyayāna*); *dolā*, *preṅkhā*, and so forth, are feminine terms for a swing.
(2.7.1039) But *dvaipavaiyāghrau* [denote] two chariots covered with the skins of leopards (*dvīpin*) and tigers (*vaiyāghra*).
(2.7.1040) A chariot covered with white woolen blankets (*pāṇḍukambala*) is called *pāṇḍukambalī*.
(2.7.1041) In the case of *kāmbalavāstrādyāḥ*, it refers to those [chariots] covered with blankets (*kambala*), cloth (*vāstra*), and so forth.
(2.7.1042) *Dvaipādayaḥ* refers to three things; *rathyā* means a carriage road, and *rathakaḍyā* means a multitude of chariots.
(2.7.1043) *Dhūḥ* is feminine, while *yānamukha* is neuter; *apaskara* is a term for a part of a chariot.
(2.7.1044) *Cakra* is a wheel, which is a part of a chariot; at its edge is the *nemi*, which is feminine, and *pradhi*, which is masculine.

(2.7.1045) *piṇḍikā* is the nave; *nābhi* and *akṣāgrakīlaka* [are synonyms]. For the two, *aṇi* [is used]. (2.7.1046) *Rathagupti* and *varūtha* are masculine; *kūbara*, however, is the yoke-pole (*yugandhara*).
(2.7.1047) *Anukarṣī* is the wooden part situated below; *prāsaṅga* is the yoke-strap (*yugādyuga*).
(2.7.1048) All [these] are synonyms for a vehicle: *vāhana*, *yāna*, *yugya*, *patra*, and *dhoraṇa*. (2.7.1049) A vehicle carried in succession is called *vainītaka* (not feminine).
(2.7.1050) *Ādhoraṇa*, *hastipaka*, *hastyāroha*, and *niṣādin* denote elephant-riders.
The *niyantṛ*, *prājita*, *yantṛ*, *sūta*, *kṣattṛ*, and *sārathi* are terms for the charioteer.
Furthermore, *savyeṣṭha* and *dakṣiṇastha* are designations for the attendants of the chariot.
Those who ride in a chariot are called *rathin* or *syandanāroha*; those who ride horses are called *aśvāroha* or *sādin*.
(2.7.1054) *Bhaṭas*, *yodhas*, and *yoddhāras* are warriors; whereas those who protect the army are *sainikas*.
(2.7.1055) Those who are assembled in the army are *sainyas*, and they are also *sainikas*.
(2.7.1056) Those who are powerful by virtue of a thousand [men] are *sāhasrās*, and they are *sahasriṇas*.
(2.7.1057) *paridhisthaḥ*, *paricaraḥ*, *senānīḥ*, and *vāhinīpatiḥ* [are synonyms for commander].

(2.7.1058) *kañcukaḥ* and *vārabāṇaḥ* (not feminine) refer to armor; that which those wearing armor fasten around their waists is (2.7.1059) *sārasanam*; furthermore, *adhikāṅgaḥ* and *śīrṣakam* [refer to headgear].

(2.7.1060) *Śīrṣaṇya* refers to a helmet; furthermore, *tanutra*, *varma*, *daṃśana*, (2.7.1061) *uraśchada*, *kaṅkaṭaka*, *jāgara*, and *kavaca*—these words for armor are not feminine. (2.7.1062) *Āmukta*, *pratimukta*, *pinaddha*, and *āpinaddha* likewise [refer to armor that has been put on].

(2.7.1063) *saṃnaddha*, *varmita*, *sajja*, *daṃśita*, and *vyuḍhakaṅkaṭa* [are synonyms for one who is armored]. (2.7.1064) The words beginning with *āmukta* apply to three genders when referring to those wearing armor; the collective term for such a group is *kāvacika*. (2.7.1065) *Padāti*, *patti*, *padaga*, *pādātika*, and *padāti* [are synonyms for a foot soldier].
(2.7.1066) A *padga* and a *padika* are those who go on foot; *pādātam* is a collection of infantry.
(2.7.1067) Among those who live by weapons, *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*, *āyudhīya*, and *āyudhika* are synonymous.
(2.7.1068) *Kṛtahasta* refers to one whose arrows are well-aimed, just like *kṛtapuṅkha*.
(2.7.1069) He whose arrow has missed the mark is *aparāddhapṛṣatka*, one from whom the shaft has slipped from the target.
(2.7.1070) An archer is called *dhanvī*, *dhanuṣmān*, *dhānuṣka*, *niṣaṅgī*, *astrī*, or *dhanurdhara*.
(2.7.1071) One who carries arrows is *kāṇḍavān* or *kāṇḍīra*; one whose weapon is a spear is *śāktīka* or *śaktihetika*.
(2.7.1072) One who has a staff (*yaṣṭi*) as a weapon is a *yāṣṭīka*, and one who has a spear (*paraśvadha*) as a weapon is a *pāraśvadhika*.

(2.7.1073) One who has a sword (*nistrimśa*) as a weapon is a *naistriṃśika*; a *prāsika* and a *kauntika* are equivalent terms for those whose weapons are the *prāsa* (javelin) and the *kunta* (lance), respectively.
(2.7.1074) A *carmī* is one who holds a shield (*phalaka*) in his hand; a *patākī* is one who possesses a banner (*vaijayantī*).

*Anuplava*, *sahāya*, *anucara*, *anucārī*, and *abhicara* are synonyms for companion or follower. *puroga*, *agresara*, *praṣṭha*, *agrataḥsara*, *puraḥsara*, and *purogama* are synonyms for one who goes before or a leader. *mandagāmī* and *manthara* refer to one who moves slowly.
*Jaṅghāla* and *atijava* are synonyms; *jaṅghākarika* and *jāṅghika* refer to one who travels on foot.
*Tarasvī*, *tvarita*, *vegī*, *prajasvī*, *javana*, and *java* denote one who is swift. *Jayya* refers to one who can be conquered; *jeya* refers to that which is merely to be conquered.
One who is victorious and goes forth fully against his enemies is called *jaitra*, *jetṛ*,
*abhyamitra*, *abhyamitrīya*, or even *abhyamitrīṇa*.
One who is endowed with an excellence of vigor is *ūrjasvala* or *ūrjasvin*.
(2.7.1084) *svāduras*, *svānurasila*, *rathika*, *rathira*, and *rathī*;
(2.7.1085) *kāmagāmin*, *anukāmīna*, and likewise *atyantīna* in the sense of "exceedingly";
(2.7.1086) *śūra*, *vīra*, and *vikrānta* mean brave; and *jetṛ*, *jiṣṇu*, and *jitvara* mean a conqueror.
(2.7.1087) *Sāṃyugīna* means one who is skilled in battle; *śastrajīva* and others [denoting those who live by weapons] apply to all three genders.
(2.7.1088) *Dhvajinī*, *vāhinī*, *senā*, *pṛtanā*, *anīkinī*, *camū*, (2.7.1089) *varūthinī*, *bala*, *sainya*, *cakra*, and *anīka* are terms for an army, with *anīka* not being feminine.

(2.7.1090) *Vyūha*, however, is the arraying of forces; its divisions in battle are the *daṇḍa* and so forth. (2.7.1091) The *pratyāsāra* is the rear (*pārṣṇi*) of the array; it is the reserve (*pratigraha*) at the back of the army.
(2.7.1092) A *patti* consists of one elephant, one chariot, three horses, and five foot soldiers.

(2.7.1093–1095) By successively multiplying all the preceding units by three, the designations for the army units are as follows: *senāmukha*, *gulma*, *gaṇa*, *vāhinī*, *pṛtanā*, *camū*, *anīkinī*, and ten *anīkinīs* constitute an *akṣauhiṇī*. Furthermore, the word *sampad* [is used in the sense of excellence].
*Saṃpattiḥ*, *śrīḥ*, and *lakṣmīḥ* denote prosperity; *vipattiḥ*, *vipat*, and *āpad* denote misfortune.
*Āyudham*, *praharaṇam*, *śastram*, and *astram* denote weapons; these two last terms are not feminine.
*Dhanuḥ*, *cāpaḥ*, *dhanva*, *śarāsanam*, *kodaṇḍaḥ*, and *kārmukam* denote a bow.
(2.7.1099) Furthermore, the bow of Karṇa is the *kālapṛṣṭha*;

(2.7.1100) the two bows of the one with the monkey-banner (*kapidhvaja*) are *gāṇḍīva* and *gāṇḍiva*, used as both masculine and neuter; (2.7.1101) its tip is the *aṭanī*; and the leather guards on the palms for warding off the friction of the bowstring are the *godhā*.

(2.7.1102) *lastaka*, however, is the middle of a bow; *maurvī*, *jyā*, *śiñjinī*, and *guṇa* are synonyms for the bowstring. (2.7.1103) *Pratyālīḍha*, *ālīḍha*, and so forth, constitute the five postures (*sthāna*).
(2.7.1104) *Lakṣya*, *lakṣa*, and *śaravya* mean a target; *śarābhyāsa* means the practice of archery.
*pṛṣatka*, *bāṇa*, *viśikha*, *ajihmaga*, *khaga*, and *āśuga* are synonyms for an arrow;
likewise, *kalamba*, *mārgaṇa*, *śara*, *patrin*, *ropa*, and *iṣu* are used for both [male and female] arrows.
However, *prakṣveḍana* and *nārāca* refer specifically to iron arrows (*nārāca*), while *pakṣa* and *vāja* apply to all three genders in the subsequent senses.
(2.7.1108) *nirasta* is used for an arrow that has been discharged; *viṣākta*, *digdha*, and *liptaka* refer to one smeared with poison.
(2.7.1109) *tūṇa*, *upāsaṅga*, *tūṇīra*, and *niṣaṅga* denote a quiver; *iṣudhi* applies to both [the quiver and its contents].
(2.7.1110) *tūṇī* refers to a quiver; whereas for a sword, there are the terms *nistriṃśa*, *candrahāsa*, *asi*, and *ṛṣṭi*.
(2.7.1111) Kaukṣeyaka, maṇḍalāgra, karavāla, and kṛpāṇa are synonyms for a sword.
(2.7.1112) Tsaru refers to the hilt of a sword or similar weapon; mekhalā is the scabbard used to bind it.
(2.7.1113) Phalaka and phala are neuter terms for a shield or leather armor; saṃgrāha is the grip or handle of such a weapon.
*Drughaṇa*, *mudgara*, and *ghana* denote a mallet; *īlī* and *karavālikā* denote a small sword.
*Bhindipāla* and *sṛga* are synonymous; *parigha* and *parighātina* denote an iron bar used as a weapon.
*Kuṭhāra*, *svadhiti*, *paraśu*, and *paraśvadha* denote an axe (the first two being masculine, the latter two neuter).

(2.7.1117) A *syā*, *śastrī*, *asiputrī*, *churikā*, and *asidhenukā* [are synonyms for a small knife]. (2.7.1118) *Śalya* and *śaṅku* may optionally be masculine; *sarvalā* and *tomara* are not feminine.
(2.7.1119) *Prāsa* and *kunta* denote a spear; *koṇa*, *pālī*, *aśri*, and *koṭi* are feminine.

(2.7.1120) *Sarvābhisāraḥ* refers to a total mobilization, a complete flood [of troops], or the purpose of full armament; (2.7.1121) *lohābhisāraḥ* is the ritual of lustration (*nīrājanā*) for kings who bear weapons; (2.7.1122) the advance of an army into a desert is called *abhiṣeṇanam*.

(2.7.1123) *Yātrā*, *vrajyā*, *abhiniryāṇa*, *prasthāna*, *gamana*, and *gama* mean going forth or marching. (2.7.1124) *Āsāra*, *prasaraṇa*, and *pracakra* signify a forward rush or an advance. (2.7.1125) *Abhikrama* is the advancing toward enemies in battle by one who is fearless.
(2.7.1126) Vaitālikas are those who awaken [the king] at dawn; ākrikas are those who carry bells, and ghāṇṭikas are those who have the same purpose.
(2.7.1127) Māgadhas are those from Magadha; they are bards (*bandins*) who recite praises.
(2.7.1128) Saṃśaptakas are those who, by a solemn vow, do not retreat from battle.
*reṇu*, *dhūli*, and *pāṃsu* (the latter two feminine) denote dust; *rajas* (neuter) is used for both [dust and passion].
(2.7.1130) *kṣoda* denotes powder; *samutpiñja* and *piñjala* mean extremely disheveled or confused.
(2.7.1131) *patākā*, *vaijayantī*, *ketana*, and *dhvaja* (masculine and neuter) denote a banner.
(2.7.1132) That battlefield where heroes are celebrated is a place that inspires great fear.
(2.7.1133) *Ahaṃpūrvikā* (feminine) refers to the state of everyone saying "I first! I first!
(2.7.1134) *Āhopuruṣikā* is the self-aggrandizement arising from pride or arrogance.
(2.7.1135) *Ahamahamikā*, however, is that mutual sense of "I am [the best].
(2.7.1136) *Draviṇa*, *taraḥ*, *sahas*, *bala*, *śaurya*, *sthāma*, and *śuṣma* denote strength.
(2.7.1137) *Śakti*, *parākrama*, and *prāṇa* denote power; *vikrama*, moreover, is the state of exceeding power.
(2.7.1138) But *vīrapāṇa* is that drinking [of wine] which occurs during an actual or impending battle;
(2.7.1139) *yuddha*, *āyodhana*, *janya*, *praghana*, *pravidāraṇa*, (2.7.1140) *mṛdha*, *āskandana*, *saṃkhya*, *samīka*, and *sāṃparāyika* [are synonyms for battle].
(2.7.1141) *samarānīkaraṇa*, *kalaha*, and *vigraha* are masculine;
(2.7.1142) *saṃprahāra*, *abhisaṃpāta*, *kali*, *saṃsphoṭa*, and *saṃyuga*;
(2.7.1143) *abhyāmarda*, *samāghāta*, *saṃgrāma*, *abhyāgama*, and *āhava* [are also masculine].

(2.7.1144) *Samudāya* refers to a group of women; *saṃyat*, *samiti*, *āji*, *samit*, and *yudh* denote battle. (2.7.1145) *Niyuddha* refers to wrestling or hand-to-hand combat; furthermore, *tumula* denotes a tumultuous or chaotic battle. (2.7.1146) *Kṣveḍā* is the lion’s roar; *ghaṭā* is a herd or gathering of elephants.
(2.7.1147) *Krandanam* is the shouting of warriors; *bṛṃhitam* is the trumpeting of elephants.
(2.7.1148) *Visphāraḥ* is the twanging of a bow; *patāhaḥ* and *ambaraḥ* are synonyms for the sound of a drum.
(2.7.1149) *Prasabham*, *balātkāraḥ*, and *haṭhaḥ* denote force; furthermore, *skhalitam* and *chalam* denote deception.
(2.7.1150) *Ajanya*, *klība*, and *utpāta*—these three are synonyms for a portentous calamity (*upasaṅga*).
(2.7.1151) *Mūrchā*, *kaśmala*, and *moha* denote fainting or stupor; *avamarda* denotes affliction or oppression.
(2.7.1152) *Abhyavaskandana* and *abhyāsādana* mean a sudden assault; *vijaya* and *jaya* mean victory.
(2.7.1153) Vairaśuddhiḥ, pratīkāraḥ, and vairaniryātanaṃ mean retaliation.
(2.7.1154) Pradrāva, uddrāva, sandrāva, sandāva, vidrava, and drava denote flight.
(2.7.1155) Apakrama and apayāna mean retreat; bhaṅga and parājaya mean defeat in battle.
(2.7.1156) *parājita* and *parābhūta* are used in three genders; *naṣṭa* and *tirohita* mean "vanished.
(2.7.1157) *pramāpaṇa*, *nibarhaṇa*, *nikāraṇa*, and *viśāraṇa*;
(2.7.1158) *pravāsana*, *parāsana*, *niṣūdana*, and *nihiṃsana*.
(2.7.1159) *nivāraṇaṃ*, *saṃjñapanam*, *nigrahaṇam*, *apāsanam*; (2.7.1160) *nistaraṇam*, *nihananam*, *kṣaṇanam*, *parivarjanam*; (2.7.1161) *nivapaṇam*, *viśasanam*, *māraṇam*, *pratighātanam*.
(2.7.1162) *udvāsana*, *pramathana*, *krathana*, and *ujjāsana*; (2.7.1163) *ālambha*, *piñja*, *viśara*, *ghāta*, *unmatha*, and *vadha* as well;
(2.7.1164) *pañcatā*, *kāladharma*, *diṣṭānta*, *pralaya*, and *atyaya* [are synonyms for death].
(2.7.1165) *anta*, *nāśa*, *mṛtyu*, *maraṇa*, and *nidhana*—these five denote death and are not feminine.
(2.7.1166–1167) *parāsu*, *prāptapañcatva*, *pareta*, *preta*, and *saṃsthita*;
*mṛta* and *pramīta*—these [seven] apply to all three genders.
*citā*, *cityā*, and *citi* are feminine terms for a funeral pyre;
*kabandha* is not feminine and refers to a headless trunk still joined with action;
*śmaśāna* and *pitṛvana* mean cemetery; and *kuṇapa* and *śava* refer to a corpse and are not feminine.
(2.7.1170) *Pragraha* and *upagraha* refer to the act of binding; *kārā* refers to a prison.
(2.7.1171) *Bhū*, *agni*, and *asu* are masculine, as are *prāṇa* and its synonyms.
*Jīva* is the preservation [of life];
*āyus* is the duration of life;
*jīvātu* is the medicine for living.
Thus ends the section on Kṣatriyas; now the section on Vaiśyas:
(2.8.1173) Ūravya, ūruja, arya, vaiśya, bhūmispṛś, and viś are synonyms for the Vaiśya.
Now, the section on Vaiśyas (2.8.1174): Ājīva, jīvikā, vārtā, vṛtti, and vartana denote livelihood.
(2.8.1175) In the feminine, agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are the modes of livelihood (vṛttayaḥ).
(2.8.1176) Service is the "dog's livelihood" (*śvavṛtti*); falsehood is "emaciation"; gleaning ears of grain and picking up single grains is "truth.
(2.8.1177) Regarding what is obtained by begging and what is obtained without begging, the terms "dead" (*mṛta*) and "immortal" (*amṛta*) apply respectively.
(2.8.1178) Trade is "truth-and-falsehood" (*satyānṛta*).
Debt (*ṛṇa*) is the lending of money; *uddhāra* is the same, while *kusīda* is the practice of lending at interest for the sake of livelihood.
That which is obtained by begging is *yācitaka*; that which is acquired through exchange is *āpamityaka*.
(2.8.1181) The creditor and the debtor are, respectively, the two parties—the lender and the receiver.
(2.8.1182) A moneylender is a *vārdhuṣika*, one who lives by interest (*vṛddhyājīva*), or a *vārdhuṣi*.
(2.8.1183) One who lives by a field is a *kārṣaka*, a *kṛṣika*, or a *kṛṣīvala*.
(2.8.1184) A field suitable for the growth of rice or paddy is called *vrīheya* or *śāleya*.
(2.8.1185) That which is the site for the cultivation of barley and so forth is called *yavya*, *yavakya*, or *yaṣṭikya*.
(2.8.1186) Just as there are the forms *tilya* and *tailīna* for sesame, there is likewise a lack of uniformity regarding *māṣa*, *umā*, and *aṇu*.
(2.8.1187) That which is capable of producing the remaining grains, such as *maudgīna* (mudga beans) and *kaudravīṇa* (kodo millet), [is called *śeṣadhānyodbhavakṣama*].
(2.8.1188) A field of vegetables and the like is called *śākaśākata* or *śākaśākin*.
(2.8.1189) However, that which has been sown with seed is *bījākṛta*; when it has been ploughed, it is *sītya*, *kṛṣṭa*, and *halyavat*.
(2.8.1190) *Triguṇākṛta*, *tṛtīyākṛta*, *trihalya*, and *trisītya* also apply to that [field].
(2.8.1191) But for a field ploughed twice (*dviguṇākṛta*), the terms *saṃvatsara*, *pūrva*, and *śambākṛta* also apply here.
(2.8.1192) Regarding sowing and so forth measured by *droṇa*, *āḍhaka*, and the like, the derivatives *drauṇika*, *āḍhakika*, and so forth are used.

(2.8.1193) One who sows a *khārī* [of grain] is called *khārīka*; these three terms—*uttama*, *ṛddha*, and *yasa*—are used in the three genders. (2.8.1194) *Vapra*, *kedāra*, and *kṣetra* are masculine and neuter; however, (2.8.1195) a field belonging to such [a group] may be called *kaidāraka*, *kaidārya*, or *kaidārika* when referring to a collection of fields.

(2.8.1196) *loṣṭa* and *leṣṭu* are masculine; [there is] *koṭiśas* and *loṣṭabhedana*. (2.8.1197) *prājana*, *todana*, and *totra* refer to a goad; *khanitra* refers to a spade or digging tool. (2.8.1198) *dātra* and *lavitra* mean a sickle; *ābandha*, *yotra*, and *yoktra* mean a tether or yoke-rope; furthermore, *phala* [means a ploughshare].
(2.8.1199) *Iṣā* is the pole, *kuṭaka* is the plowshare, *phāla* is the plowshare, *kṛṣaka* is the plowman, and *lāṅgala* as well as *hala* are the plow.
(2.8.1200) *Godāraṇa* and *sīra* also mean plow; furthermore, *śamyā* is the female [term] for the pin of the yoke (*yugakīlaka*).
(2.8.1201) *Īṣā* is the shaft of the plow, and *sītā* is the furrow made by the plow.
(2.8.1202) *Medhi* (masc. is the wooden post set in the threshing floor for binding animals;
(2.8.1203) *āśu* is a type of rice, while *pāṭala* refers to red rice; *śitaśūka* and *yava* denote barley;
(2.8.1204) *tokma* is the green sprout of that [barley], while *kalāya* and *satīnaka* refer to the pea.
In this [section], *hareṇu* and *eṇuka* are mentioned; *koradūṣa*, however, is *kodrava*.
(2.8.1206) *Maṅgalyaka* is *masūra*; then there are *makuṣṭhaka* and *mayuṣṭhaka*. (2.8.1207) For the wild bean (*vanamudga*), there are two names: *taṃtubha* and *kadambaka*.
(2.8.1208) *siddhārtha* is white mustard; *godhūma* and *sumana* are synonyms for wheat.
(2.8.1209) *yāvaka* and *kulmāṣa* refer to half-cooked barley; *caṇaka* and *harimanthaka* are synonyms for chickpeas.
(2.8.1210) *tilapeja* and *tilapiñja* are two terms for a sesame seed that has lost its oil.
(2.8.1211) *Kṣavaḥ* is that which produces sneezing; *rājikā*, *kṛṣṇikā*, and *āsurī* refer to black mustard.
(2.8.1212) *Kaṅgu* and *priyaṅgu* are two [names for millet]; *atasī*, *umā*, and *kṣumā* are synonyms for linseed.
(2.8.1213) *Mātulānī* refers to hemp (*bhaṅgā*); *aṇu* is a variety of rice and is masculine.
*Kiṃśāru* is the awn of a grain; *kaṇiśa* is the ear of grain.
(2.8.1215) *Dhānya*, *vrīhi*, and *stambakari* refer to grain; *stamba* is a cluster of grass and the like.
(2.8.1216) *Nāḍī* and *nāla* denote its stalk (*kāṇḍa*); *palāla* is that same stalk when it is without fruit (husked).
(2.8.1217) *Kaḍaṅgara* is chaff, used in the neuter; *tuṣa*, however, is the husk of grain and is masculine.
(2.8.1218) *Śūka* is not feminine and refers to a fine, sharp point; *śamī* and *śimbā* [refer to the pod] and apply to the three [preceding genders] in the following senses.
(2.8.1219) *Ṛddha* and *āvasita* refer to threshed grain; *pūta* refers to that which has been winnowed or cleaned.
(2.8.1220) Māṣa and others are pulse-grains (*śamīdhānya*); barley and others are awned-grains (*śūkadhānya*).
(2.8.1221) Rice (*śāli*), *kalama* and the like, and *ṣaṣṭika* and the like—these are masculine.
(2.8.1222) Grass-grains are *nīvāra*; *gavedhu* and *gavedhukā* are feminine.

(2.8.1223) *Ayogra* and *musala* denote a pestle (the latter is not feminine); *udūkhalam* and *ulūkhalam* denote a mortar. (2.8.1224) *Prasphoṭanam*, *śūrpaḥ* (masculine), and *cālanī* denote a winnowing fan; *titauḥ* (masculine) denotes a sieve. (2.8.1225) *Syūta* and *praseva* denote a sack; *kaṇḍola*, *piṭa*, *kaṭa*, and *kiliñjaka* denote a basket or mat.
(2.8.1226) *Rasavatī* and *pākasthāna* and *mahānasa* are synonyms for the kitchen.
(2.8.1227) *Paurogava* is the superintendent thereof; *sūpakāra*, *ballava*, (2.8.1228) *ārālika*, *āndhasika*, *sūda*, *audanika*, and *guṇa* are terms for cooks.
(2.8.1229) An *āpūpika* (maker of cakes), a *kāndavika* (seller of fried snacks), and a *bhakṣyakāra* (maker of eatables)—these three [terms] refer to the same person.
(2.8.1230) *Aśmanta*, *uddhāna*, *adhiśrayaṇī*, *culli*, and *antikā* (all denote a hearth).
(2.8.1231) *Aṅgāradhānikā*, *aṅgāraśakaṭī*, and *hasantī* (all denote a charcoal tray).
(2.8.1232) *Hasantī* may also be used for a female [fire-drill], while *aṅgāra*, *alāta*, and *ulmuka* denote a charcoal fire.
(2.8.1233) *Ambarīṣa* and *bhrāṣṭra* are neuter; *kandu* is masculine, or *svedanī* is feminine.
(2.8.1234) *Aliñjara* and *maṇika* refer to a large water-jar; *karṛru* and *galantikā* refer to a small water-drip vessel.
*Piṭhara*, *sthālī*, *ukhā*, and *kuṇḍa* denote a cooking pot; *kalaśa*, however, is used in three genders, while [the others] are in two.
(2.8.1236) *Ghaṭa*, *kuṭa*, and *nipa* are not feminine; *śarāva* and *vṛmānaka* denote a shallow dish.
(2.8.1237) *Ṛjīṣa* is a vessel for baking flour; *kaṃsa* is not feminine and denotes a drinking vessel.
(2.8.1238) *Kutū* is a vessel for oil used for cutting; that same vessel when small is called *kutupa*, which is masculine.
(2.8.1239) *Savarmāvapana*, *bhāṇḍa*, *pātra*, *amatra*, and *bhājana* are synonyms for a container or vessel.
(2.8.1240) *Daṛiḥ*, *kambiḥ*, and *khajākā* are synonyms for a ladle; *dārūdūra* is a wooden ladle.
(2.8.1241) *Śāka* and *haritaka* are not feminine; its stalk is called *śigru*.
(2.8.1242) *Kalamba*, *kadamba*, *veṣavāra*, and *upaskara* [are synonyms for spices].
(2.8.1243) *Tintiḍīka*, *cukra*, and *vṛkṣāmla* are synonyms for the tamarind tree; furthermore, *vellaja* [is another name for it].
Marīca, kolaka, kṛṣṇabhūṣaṇa, and dhṛpattana are synonyms for black pepper.
Jīraka, jaraṇa, ajāji, and kaṇā refer to cumin; however, when specifically black, it is called jīraka.
Suṣavī, kāravī, pṛthvī, pṛthu, and kālopakuñcikā are synonyms for caraway.

Ārdraka and śṛṅgabera are synonyms for fresh ginger; then chatrā and vitunnaka are synonyms for cumin; kustumburu and dhānyāka are synonyms for coriander; and śuṇṭhī, mahauṣadha, viśva, nāgara, and viśvabheṣaja are synonyms for dry ginger (used in both feminine and neuter genders).
Āranālaka, sauvīraka, kulmāṣābhiṣuta, and the fermented liquors known as avantisoma, dhānyāmla, and kuñjala are synonyms for kāñjika.
Sahasravedhi, jatuka, balhīka, hiṅgu, and rāmaṭha are synonyms for asafoetida.
(2.8.1253) *tatpatrī*, *kāravī*, *pṛthvī*, *bāṣpikā*, *kabarī*, and *pṛthu*;
(2.8.1254) *niśākhyā*, *kāñcanī*, *pītā*, *haridrā*, and *varavarṇinī*.
(2.8.1255) That which is ocean-born salt (*sāmudralavaṇa*) is also called *akṣīva* and *vaśira*.
*Saindhava* (rock salt) is not feminine; it is also called *śītaśiva*, *māṇimantha*, and *sindhuja*.
*Raumaka*, *vasuka*, *pākya*, and *biḍa* are two types of artificial salts.
*Sauvarcala* is also called *akṣarucaka*; when it is dark-colored, it is called *tilaka*.
(2.8.1259) *Matsyaṇḍī* is unrefined sugar; *phāṇita* is molasses; *śarkarā* and *sitā* are varieties of candied sugar.

(2.8.1260) *Kūrcikā* is a preparation of milk; *rasālā*, however, is *mārjitā*. (2.8.1261) *Temana* and *niṣṭhāna* refer to seasoned dishes; these terms, up to the word *vāsitā*, are of three genders.
(2.8.1262) *Śūlākṛta* and *bhaṭitra* refer to meat cooked on a spit; *śūlya* is the primary term for this, while *paiṭhara* refers to food cooked in a pot.

(2.8.1263) *Praṇīta*, *upasaṃpanna*, and *prayasta* denote that which is well-prepared or well-refined. (2.8.1264) *Picchila* and *vijila* are synonyms for slippery or slimy; *saṃmṛṣṭa* and *śodhita* are equivalent terms meaning cleansed or swept.
(2.8.1265) *Cikkaṇa*, *masṛṇa*, and *snigdha* are synonyms; likewise are *bhāvita* and *vāsita*.
(2.8.1266) *Āpakva* is [the same as] *pauli*; *abhyūṣa* is [the same as] *lāja*; and *akṣata* is used in the masculine plural.
(2.8.1267) *Pṛthuka* is *cipiṭaka*; *dhānā* refers to roasted barley, and is feminine in the plural.

(2.8.1268) *Pūpa*, *apūpa*, and *piṣṭaka* denote a cake; *karambha* refers to groats mixed with curd. (2.8.1269) *Bhissā*, *bhakta*, *andhas*, *anna*, and *odana*—the last being masculine—are terms for cooked rice; it is also called *dīdivi*. (2.8.1270) *Bhissaṭā* and *dagdhikā* refer to burnt rice; *maṇḍa* is the scum of boiled rice and is not feminine.

The scum produced from boiled rice is called *māsarā*, *ācāma*, or *nisrāva*. The thick liquid arising from cooked rice is *maṇḍa*. *Yavāgū*, *uṣṇikā*, *śrāṇā*, *vilepī*, and *taralā* all refer to thin gruel.
*Mrakṣaṇa* and *abhyañjana* denote oil for smearing or anointing. *Kṛsara* is rice cooked with sesame seeds.
(2.8.1274) *gavya* is used in three genders for everything pertaining to cows; *go-viṭ* (cow-dung) and *go-maya* (cow-made) are feminine.
(2.8.1275) When dried, that is called *karīṣa*, which is not feminine; *dugdha*, *kṣīra*, and *payaḥ* are synonymous.
(2.8.1276) *Payasya* refers to clarified butter (*ājya*), curds (*dadhi*), and so forth; *trapsya* is curds that are not thick.
Ghṛta, ājya, havis, and sarpi are synonyms for clarified butter; navanīta is fresh butter just extracted from cream.
That ghee which is produced from the milk of a cow that has calved for the first time is called haiyaṅgavīna.
Dandāhata, kālaśeya, and ariṣṭa are also names for the liquid product of the cow (gorasa).
(2.8.1280) *Takram* is buttermilk; *udaśvit* is churned [curd] with one part water; *pādāmbu* is [curd] with one-quarter water; *nirjala* is [curd] without water.
(2.8.1281) *Maṇḍa* is the whey produced from curd; *mastu* is the same; *pīyūṣa* is fresh milk.
(2.8.1282) *Aśanāyā*, *bubhukṣā*, and *kṣut* denote hunger; *grāsa*, however, is a mouthful (masculine).
(2.8.1283) *Sapītiḥ* is a feminine noun meaning drinking together; *sagdhiḥ* is a feminine noun meaning eating together.
(2.8.1284) *Udanyā*, *pipāsā*, and *tṛṭ* mean thirst; *tarpaḥ*, *jagdhiḥ*, and *bhojanam* mean eating.
(2.8.1285) *Jemanam*, *lehaḥ*, *āhāraḥ*, *nighāsaḥ*, and *nyādaḥ* also denote food or the act of eating.
(2.8.1286) *Sauhitya*, *tarpaṇa*, and *tṛpti* mean satiety; *phelā* is that which is left over after eating.
(2.8.1287) *Kāmam*, *prakāmam*, *paryāptam*, *nikāmam*, *iṣṭam*, and *yathepsitam* mean according to one's desire or wish.
(2.8.1288) *Gopa*, *gopāla*, *gosamkhya*, *godhuk*, *ābhīra*, and *vallava* are synonyms for a cowherd.
(2.8.1289) A tethering post for cattle, buffaloes, and so forth is called *gavīśvara*.
(2.8.1290) One who possesses cows is *gomān* or *gomī*; a herd of cows is *gokula*, *godhana*, or *gavāṃ vraja*.
(2.8.1291) *Āśitaṃgavīna* (three genders) refers to a place where cows have previously been fed.
(2.8.1292) *Ukṣan*, *bhadra*, *balīvarda*, *ṛṣabha*, *vṛṣabha*, and *vṛṣa* [mean] a bull.
(2.8.1293) *Anaḍvān*, *saurabheya*, and *go* [mean] a bull; a collection of bulls is *aukṣakam*.
(2.8.1294) *Gavyā* and *gotrā* [mean] a herd of cows; *vātsaka* [denotes] a herd of calves, and *dhainuka* [denotes] a herd of milch-cows.
A large bull is called *ukṣā* or *mahokṣaḥ*; an old bull, however, is *vṛddhokṣaḥ* or *jaradgavaḥ*. A bull that has recently calved is *jātokṣaḥ*; one just born is *tarṇakaḥ*.
A calf that voids dung is *śakṛtkariḥ*; the terms *damyaḥ* and *vatsataraḥ* are synonymous.

(2.8.1298) *Ārṣabhya* refers to one fit for castration; a *ṣaṇḍa* is a bull that wanders alone. (2.8.1299) A *vaha* is one that carries its own load on the shoulder; *sāsnā*, however, is the dewlap on the neck.
(2.8.1300) *Nastita* means one led by a nose-string; a *praṣṭhavāṭ* is one that walks at the side of the yoke.

(2.8.1301) Those who carry the yoke and so forth are called *yugya*, *prāsaṅgya*, and *śākaṭa*. (2.8.1302) One who digs with something is called *hālika* (a plowman), and one who carries that [load] is called *sairika* (a sower). (2.8.1303) One who bears the burden is called *dhurya*, *dhaureya*, *dhurīṇa*, and *dhurandhara*.
(2.8.1304) Both *ekadhurīṇa* and *ekadhura* mean "bearing a single yoke" (*ekadhurāvahe*). (2.8.1305) But he who indeed bears every yoke is called *sarvadhurīṇa*.
(2.8.1306) A cow is called *māheyī*, *saurabheyī*, *gauḥ*, *usrā*, *mātā*, and *śṛṅgiṇī*.
(2.8.1307) *Arjunī*, *aghnī*, and *rohiṇī* are terms for an excellent cow among cattle; *naucikī* refers to one that is not so.
(2.8.1308) Based on distinctions of color and other traits, there are designations such as *śabalī* (variegated), *dhavalā* (white), and so forth.
(2.8.1309) A two-year-old cow is called *dvihāyanī*; a one-year-old cow is *ekahāyanī*.
A four-year-old cow is called *caturhāyanī*, and likewise, a three-year-old cow is *trihāyaṇī*.

A barren cow is *vaśā*; one that has miscarried is *avatokā*; one whose fetus is leaking is *sravadgarbhā*; one that is in heat is *sandhinī*; one covered by a bull is *ākrāntā*; and one that destroys the embryo is *vehat*.

(2.8.1313) A cow that comes into heat at the proper time for breeding is called *praṣṭhauhī* when she is pregnant with her first calf. (2.8.1314) One who is not fierce is *sukarā*; one who has many offspring is *pareṣṭukā*. (2.8.1315) A cow that has calved long ago is *baṣkayaṇī*, while one that has recently calved is *dhenu*.
(2.8.1316) *Suvratā* is one who is easy to satisfy; *pīnodhnī* is one with a full udder; *pīvarastanī* is one with large breasts.
(2.8.1317) *Droṇakṣīrā* is one that yields a *droṇa* measure of milk; *droṇadugdhā* is the same; *dhenuṣyā* is a cow held as a pledge.
(2.8.1318) *Samāṃsamīnā* is she who gives birth every year.

(2.8.1319) *Ūdhas* is neuter; *āpīna* is also [a term for the udder]. *Śivaka* and *kīlaka* are synonyms [for a wooden peg]. (2.8.1320) *Dāma* and *sandāna* are not masculine [though they may be used as such]; *paśurajju*, however, is *dāmanī*.
(2.8.1321) *Vaiśākha*, *mantha*, and *manthāna* refer to the churning vessel; *manthāna* also refers to the churning stick.
*Kuṭhara*, *daṇḍaviṣkambha*, *manthanī*, and *gargarī* are synonyms for a churning vessel.
*Kramelaka*, *maya*, *mahāṅga*, and *karabha* denote a camel; *karabha* also refers to its young.
Young camels (*karabhāḥ*) are called *śṛṅkhalakāḥ* when their feet are bound with wooden fetters.
(2.8.1325) *ajā* means a she-goat; *śubha*, *chāga*, *basta*, and *chagalaka* also mean a goat.
(2.8.1326) *meḍhra*, *urabhra*, *uraṇa*, *ūrṇāyu*, *meṣa*, and *vṛṣṇi* denote a ram; *eḍaka* denotes a sheep.
(2.8.1327) A herd of camels, rams, or goats is respectively called *auṣṭraka*, *aurabhra*, or *ājaka*.
(2.8.1328) Cakrīvantaḥ, vāleyāḥ, rāsabhāḥ, gardabhāḥ, and kharāḥ are synonyms for donkey.
(2.8.1329–1330) A vaidehaka, sārthavāha, naigama, vāṇija, vaṇij, paṇyājīva, āpaṇika, and krayavikrayika are all terms for a merchant.
(2.8.1331) One who sells is a *vikretṛ*, while a *vikrayika* is the same; *krāyika* and *krayika* are synonymous.
(2.8.1332) Trade is *vāṇijya* or *vaṇijyā*; price is *mūlya*, *vasna*, or *avakraya*.
(2.8.1333) *Nīvī* is the capital or principal wealth (*paripaṇa*, *mūladhana*); profit is the surplus fruit (*lābha*, *adhika-phala*).

(2.8.1334) *Paridāna*, *parīvarta*, *naimeya*, and *niyama* [denote exchange]. (2.8.1335) *Upanidhi* and *nyāsa* are masculine [and denote a deposit]; *pratidāna* is the returning of that. (2.8.1336) That which is displayed for sale at a market is *krayya*; *kreya* and *kretavya* refer to anything merely fit to be bought.
(2.8.1337) *vikreyam*, *paṇitavyam*, and *paṇyam* mean "to be sold"; *krayya* and others are used in all three genders.
(2.8.1338) In the neuter, *satyāpanam*, *satyaṅkāraḥ*, and *satyākṛtiḥ* (in the feminine) mean "the act of making true" or "an oath.
(2.8.1339) *Vipaṇaḥ* means "selling"; numbers from one up to ten are used in all three genders when they qualify a countable object (*saṃkhyeya*).
(2.8.1340) The words beginning with *viṃśati* (twenty) are always singular, whether they denote the number itself or the thing numbered.
(2.8.1341) When used in the sense of a number, they may take dual or plural endings; among them, those ending in *-anavati* are feminine.
(2.8.1342) From *paṅkti* onwards, the series of *śata*, *sahasra*, and so forth, increases tenfold at each step.
(2.8.1343) *yautava*, *druvaya*, and *pāyya*—these three denote measures.
(2.8.1344) Measurement is by means of scales, finger-breadths, and *prasthas*; five *guñjās* and so forth constitute a *māṣaka*.
(2.8.1345) Sixteen of those make an *akṣa* or *karṣa* (the latter not feminine); four *karṣas* make a *pala*.
(2.8.1346) Two *suvarṇas* make a *bista* of gold; a *kurubista*, however, is a *pala* of that [silver].
(2.8.1347) A *tulā* is a hundred *palas* in the feminine gender; twenty *tulās* would be a *bhāra*. (2.8.1348) Ten *bhāras* would be an *ācita*; a cartload (*śākaṭa*) is a *bhāra* that is an *ācita*.

(2.8.1349) A *kārṣāpaṇa* may be called *kārṣika*; a copper coin weighing one *karṣa* is a *paṇa*. (2.8.1350–1351) *Āḍhaka*, *droṇa*, *khārī*, *vāha*, and *nikuñcaka*—these, as well as *kuḍava*, *prastha*, and so forth, are distinct terms denoting measures of capacity.
A fourth part is a *pāda*; however, *aṃśa* and *bhāga* refer to a share or portion.
*Dravya*, *vitta*, *svāpateya*, *riktha*, *ṛktha*, *dhana*, *vasu*, *hiraṇya*, *draviṇa*, *dyumna*, *artha*, *rai*, and *vibhava* are synonyms for wealth.

(2.8.1355) There may be *kośa* and *hiraṇya*; gold and silver, whether wrought or unwrought; (2.8.1356) whatever is other than those two is called *kupya*. That which is wrought from those two is *rūpya*. (2.8.1357) *Gārutmata*, *marakata*, *aśmagarbha*, and *harinmaṇi* [are gems].
(2.8.1358) *Śoṇaratna* (red gem), *lohitaka*, and *padmarāga* denote ruby; then *mauktika* (pearl);

(2.8.1359) *muktā* (pearl); then *vidruma*; *pravāla* is masculine, while [the same word] is neuter; (2.8.1360) *ratna* and *maṇi* are used for both genders when referring to a species of stone, as well as for pearls and the like.
Svarṇa, suvarṇa, kanaka, hiraṇya, and hemakāṭaka; tapanīya, śātakumbha, gāṅgeya, bharma, and karvura;
cāmīkara, jātarūpa, mahārajata, and kāñcana [are synonyms for gold].
(2.8.1364) *rukma*, *kārtasvara*, *jāmbūnada*, and *aṣṭāpada* are synonyms for gold, used in the neuter gender.
(2.8.1365) That which is gold for ornaments is called *śṛṅgīkanaka*.
(2.8.1366) *Durvarṇa*, *rajata*, *rūpya*, *kharjūra*, and *śveta* are synonyms for silver.
*Rīti* (bronze) is feminine; *ārakūṭa* (also bronze) is not feminine. Then *tāmraka* (copper), *śulba*, *mlecchamukha*, *dvyaṣṭa*, *variṣṭa*, and *udumbara* [are synonyms for copper].
*Loha* (iron), which is not feminine, is also called *śastraka*, *tīkṣṇa*, *piṇḍa*, *kālāyasa*, and *ayasa*.

(2.8.1370) *Aśmasāra* and *maṇḍūra* denote iron; *siṃhāṇa* refers to its impurity. (2.8.1371) All that is metallic is called *lauha*; a derivative of iron is *kuśī*. (2.8.1372) *Kṣāra*, *kāca*, *capala*, *rasa*, *sūta*, and *pārada* refer to mercury.
(2.8.1373) *Gavala* is the horn of a buffalo; *abhraka* is the pure mineral from the mountains. (2.8.1374) *Srotoñjana* is *maurvīra*; *kāpotāñjana* and *yāmuna* are [other types of] collyrium.
(2.8.1375) *Tutthāñjana*, *śikhigrīva*, *vitunnaka*, and *mayūraka* are [synonyms for] blue vitriol.
Karparī, dāviṅkā, and kākoda are synonyms for *tuttha*.
*Rasāñjana* is also known as *rasagarbha* and *tārkṣyaśaila*. *Gandhāśman* is called *gandhika* and *saugandhika*. *Cakṣuṣyā*, *kulālī*, and *kulatthikā* are synonyms.

(2.8.1379) *rītipuṣpa*, *puṣpaka*, *puṣpaka*, and *kusumāñjana*; (2.8.1380) *piñjara*, *pītana*, *tāla*, *māla*, and *haritālaka* [are synonyms for yellow orpiment]; (2.8.1381) *gaireya*, *ārthya*, *girija*, and *aśmaja* [are synonyms for] *śilājatu*.
(2.8.1382) *vola*, *gandharasa*, *prāṇa*, *piṇḍa*, and *goparasa* are synonyms [for mercury].
(2.8.1383) *Ḍiṇḍīra*, *abdhikapha*, and *phena* denote sea-foam; *sindūra* and *nāgasaṃbhava* denote vermilion.
(2.8.1384) *Nāga*, *sīsaka*, *yogeṣṭa*, and *vaprā* refer to lead; *piñcaṭa* is used in all three genders.
(2.8.1385) Raṅga and vaṅga; then picu, tūla, and kamalottara (2.8.1386); kusumbha, vahniśikha, and mahārajana (2.8.1387) are synonyms for safflower.
Meṣakambala, ūrṇāyu, and śaśorṇa denote the wool of a rabbit (śaśaloman).
(2.8.1388) *Madhu* refers to honey, such as that produced by bees (*mākṣika*) and so forth; *madhūcchiṣṭa*, however, is beeswax (*sikthaka*).
(2.8.1389) *Manaḥśilā*, *manoguptā*, *manohvā*, and *nāgajihvikā* [are synonyms for realgar].
(2.8.1390) *Naipālī*, *kunaṭī*, and *golā* [are synonyms for orpiment]; *yavakṣāra* is *yavāgraja*.
(2.8.1391) *Pākya*, as well as *sarjikākṣāra*, *kāpota*, and *sukhavarcaka*;
(2.8.1392) *sauvarcala* and *rucaka*; *tvakkṣīrī* and *vaṃśarocanā*; (2.8.1393) *śigruja*, *śvetamarica*, *moraṭa*, and *aikṣava-mūla*.
Granthika is pippalīmūla, also known as caṭikāśiras; golomī is bhūtakeśa; patrāṅga is raktacandana; trikaṭu, tryūṣaṇa, and vyopa are synonyms for the three pungents; and triphalā is phalatrika.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Section on Vaiśyas; herein there are 111 root verses.
Now begins the Section on Śūdras.
(2.8.1397) Śūdras, those of the lowest caste, vṛṣalas, and those born of low birth;
now begins the section on Śūdras (2.8.1398).
From the Caṇḍāla downwards, there are mixed castes such as the Ambaṣṭhas, Karanas, and others.
From a Śūdra man and a Vaiśya woman is born a Karaṇa; from a Vaiśya man and a twice-born woman is born an Ambaṣṭha.
From a Śūdra man and a Kṣatriya woman is born an Ugra; from a Kṣatriya man and a Vaiśya woman is born a Māgadha.
From a Vaiśya man and a Kṣatriya woman is born a Māhiṣya; from a Vaiśya man and a Śūdra woman is born a Kṣattṛ.
From a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇī woman is born a Sūta; from a Vaiśya on that same woman is born a Vaidehaka.
A Rathakāra, however, is he whose birth is from a Māhiṣya father and a Karaṇī mother. And a Caṇḍāla is he who is begotten by a Śūdra on a Brāhmaṇī woman.
A *kāru* is an artisan; a group of such people of the same caste joined together is called a *śreṇi*.
A *kulaka* is the head of a guild (*kulaśreṣṭhin*). A florist is a *mālākāra*, while a potter is a *kumbhakāra* or *kulāla*. A plasterer is a *palagaṇḍa*.
A weaver is called *tantuvāya* or *kuvinda*, while a tailor is a *tunnavāya* or *saucauka*. A painter who lives by his craft is a *raṅgājīva* or *citrakara*, and a sword-polisher is an *asi-dhāvaka*.
A shoemaker is a *pādakṛt* or *carmakāra*, and an ironworker is a *vyokāra* or *lohakāraka*.
(2.8.1411) A *nāḍindhama* is a goldsmith; a *kalāda* is a worker in gold.
(2.8.1412) A *śāṅkhika* is a worker in shells, a *kāmbavika* is a worker in conch, and a *śaulbika* is a worker in copper (*tāmrakuṭṭaka*).
(2.8.1413) A *takṣan*, however, is a carpenter (*vardhakin*), a *tvaṣṭṛ*, a chariot-maker (*rathakāra*), and a wood-worker (*kāṣṭhataṭ*).

(2.8.1414) A village carpenter is one who is dependent on the village; a forest carpenter (*kauṭatakṣa*) is one who is not dependent. (2.8.1415) A razor-bearer (*kṣurī*), a shaver (*muṇḍī*), a "one praised by day" (*divākīrti*), a barber (*nāpita*), and a low-caste worker (*antāvasāyin*).
(2.8.1416) A washerman is a *nirṇejaka* or a *rajaka*; a vintner is a *śauṇḍika* or a *maṇḍahāraka*.
Jābāla is one who lives by goats; Devala is one who lives by the gods.
Śāmbarī is illusion; a magician is called a *pratihāraka*.
Those who live by their wives are *śailālins*, *śailūṣas*, and *kṛśāśvins*.
(2.8.1420) Actors are called *bharatas*, while wandering performers are *cāraṇas* or *kuśīlavas*.
(2.8.1421) Drummers are *mārdaṅgikas* or *maurajikas*, while those who clap their hands are *pāṇivādas* or *pāṇighās*.
(2.8.1422) Flute players are *veṇudhmās* or *vaiṇavikas*, while lute players are *vīṇāvādas* or *vaiṇikas*.
A fowler who ends the lives of living beings is called a *śākunika*; a trapper and a net-caster are two other types.
A bird-catcher, a snare-setter, and a meat-seller—these three are synonymous.
A hired laborer, one who subsists on wages, a manual worker, and a salaried servant are also the same.
A news-bearer is a *vaivadhika*, while a carrier of loads is a *bhārika*.
One who is discolored, base, lowly, vulgar, and a commoner is a *pṛthagjana*.
He is also called *nihīna*, *apasada*, *jālma*, *kṣullaka*, and *itara*.

(2.8.1429) *bhṛtya*, *dāsera*, *dāseya*, *dāsa*, *gopyaka*, and *ceṭaka*; (2.8.1430) *niyojya*, *kiṅkara*, *praiṣya*, *bhujiṣya*, and *paricāraka*; (2.8.1431) *parācita*, *pariskanda*, *parajāta*, and *paraidhita*.
(2.8.1432) *mānda*, *tuṇḍaparimṛja*, *ālasya*, *śītaka*, *alasa*, and *anuṣṇa* denote one who is lazy.
(2.8.1433) *dakṣa*, *catura*, *peśala*, *paṭu*, *sūtthāna*, and *uṣṇa* denote one who is clever or dexterous.
(2.8.1434) *caṇḍāla*, *plava*, *mātaṅga*, *divākīrti*, and *janaṅgama* denote an outcaste.
(2.8.1435) Nipāda, aśvapaca, antevāsin, cāṇḍāla, and pukkasas are [sub-]varieties.
(2.8.1436) Kirāta, śabara, and pulinda are tribes of Mlecchas.
(2.8.1437) A hunter who lives by killing deer is called a vyādha; he is also known as a mṛgayu or a lubdhaka.
Kauleyaka, sārameya, kukkura, and mṛgadaṃśaka;

śunaka, bhapaka, and śvā—these are synonyms for a dog. However, that which is devoid of rabies (alarka) is called a *yogita*. A hunting dog skilled in the chase is a *viśvakadru*, while a female dog is a *saramā*.

(2.8.1441) A village pig is called *viṭcara*; a young goat is a *varkara*, a young animal. (2.8.1442) *Ācchodana* and *mṛgavya* denote hunting; *ākheṭa* and *mṛgayā* (the latter feminine) also mean hunting.
(2.8.1443) A deer that has been struck by a poisoned arrow is called *dakṣiṇerma*.
(2.8.1444) *caura*, *ekāgārika*, *stena*, *dasyu*, *taskara*, and *upakā* are synonyms for thief.
(2.8.1445) *pratirodhin*, *parāskandin*, *pāṭaccara*, and *malimluca* are also [synonyms].
(2.8.1446) *caurikā*, *stainya*, and *caurya* denote theft; *steya* is also used in this sense, while *loptra* refers to the stolen property itself.
*vītaṃsa* is the apparatus for binding deer and birds;
*unmātha* is a concealed snare, while *vāgurā* is a net for catching deer.
*Śulba* and *varāṭaka* are synonyms; however, *rajju* is feminine, whereas *vaṭī* and *guṇa* are used in all three genders.
(2.8.1450) *Udghāṭanam*, *ghaṭīyantram*, and *salilodvāhanam* refer to a water-wheel for lifting water from a well.
(2.8.1451) *Vemā* and *vāyadaṇḍaḥ* are masculine; *sūtrāṇi* and *tantavaḥ* (threads) are masculine.
(2.8.1452) *Vāṇiḥ* and *vyūtiḥ* are feminine and synonymous; *pustam* refers to work such as plastering or modeling.

(2.8.1453) A *pāñcālikā* is a doll made of cloth, ivory, or other materials; (2.8.1454) whereas objects fashioned from lac or tin are respectively called *jātupa* and *trāpuṣa*, used in the three genders; (2.8.1455) *piṭaka*, *peṭaka*, *peṭā*, and *mañjūṣā* denote a chest or casket, while *vihaṅgikā* refers to a small basket or carrier.
A carrying-pole (*bhārayaṣṭi*) is that to which a sling (*śikya*) is suspended; a net-bag (*kāca*) and a sandal (*pādukā*) are also so called.
A woman's shoe is called *pādū* or *upānat*; when it reaches up to the ankle, it is specifically termed *anupadīnā*.
A leather thong is called *naddhī*, *vardhī*, or *varatrā*; a whip for striking horses and the like is a *kaśā*.
The *caṇḍālikā* is a lute made from a basket; it is also called a *caṇḍālavallakī*. A *nārācī* is an arrow; an *eṣaṇikā* is a probe. *Śāṇa*, *nikaṣa*, and *kaṣa* refer to a touchstone.
A *vraścana* is a leaf-shaped axe; *īpikā* and *tūlikā* are synonyms for a brush.
(2.8.1462) *taijasāvartanī*, *mūṣā*, *bhastrā*, and *carmaprasevikā* [are synonyms for a crucible].
(2.8.1463) *āsphoṭanī*, *vedhanikā*, *kṛpāṇī*, and *kartarī* are synonymous.
(2.8.1464) *vṛkṣādanī*, *vṛkṣabhedī*, *ṭaṅkaḥ*, and *pāṣāṇadāraṇaḥ* [are synonyms for a chisel].

(2.8.1465) *Krakaca* is not feminine; it means a saw (*karapatra*) or a chisel (*ārā*), as well as a tool for piercing leather. (2.8.1466) *Sūrmī* refers to a pillar or an iron image. *Śilpa* denotes work, such as the fine arts and so forth.
(2.8.1467) *Pratimāna*, *pratibimba*, *pratimā*, *pratiyātanā*, and *praticchāyā* all mean a likeness or a reflection.
(2.8.1468) *pratikṛti*, *arcā*, and *pratinidhi* are masculine; *upamā* and *upamāna* are [neuter].

(2.8.1469–1470) *vācyaliṅga* (agreeing with the gender of the referent), *sama*, *tulya*, *sadṛkṣa*, *sadṛśa*, *sadṛk*, *sādhāraṇa*, and *samāna*—these [terms] [are used] when followed by a subsequent word (*uttarapada*).
(2.8.1471) *nibha*, *saṃkāśa*, *nīkāśa*, *pratīkāśa*, *upama*, and so forth;
(2.8.1472) *karmaṇyā*, *vidhā*, *bhṛtyā*, *bhṛti*, and *bharma* denote wages (*vetana*); (2.8.1473) *bharaṇya*, *bharaṇa*, *mūlya*, *nirveśa*, and *paṇa* are also used in this sense.
*Surā*, *halipriyā*, *hālā*, *parisrut*, and *varuṇātmajā* are synonyms for liquor.
*Gandhottamā*, *prasannā*, *īrā*, *kādambarī*, and *parisrutā* refer to distilled spirits.
*Madirā* and *kaśya* denote intoxicating drinks; furthermore, *avadaṃśa* refers to a snack or appetizer.
(2.8.1477) *śuṇḍāpānam*, *madasthānam*, *madhuvārāḥ*, and *madhukramāḥ* [refer to drinking sessions].
(2.8.1478) *madhvāsavaḥ*, *mādhavakaḥ*, *madhu*, and *mādhvīkam* [are synonyms] for honey-wine (*madhu*).
(2.8.1479) *maireyaḥ*, *āsavaḥ*, *sīdhuḥ*, *mandakaḥ*, and *jagalaḥ* are synonymous.

(2.8.1480) *Sandhāna* and *abhiṣava* refer to the process of fermentation; *kiṇva* is yeast, while *nagnahūḥ* is masculine. (2.8.1481) *Surāmaṇḍa* ending in *kāra* refers to the scum of liquor; *āpāna* is a drinking party or social gathering.
(2.8.1482) *Capaka* (not feminine) is a drinking vessel; *saraka* and *anutarṣaṇa* also denote a drinking vessel.

(2.8.1483) *dhūrta*, *akṣadevin*, *kitava*, *akṣadhūrta*, and *dyūtakṛt* are synonyms for a gambler. (2.8.1484) *lagnaka*, *pratibhū*, *sabhika*, and *dyūtakāraka* refer to those who act as guarantors or keepers of the gambling hall. (2.8.1485) *Dyūta* (in the non-feminine gender), *akṣavatī*, *kaitava*, and *paṇa* denote gambling.

(2.8.1486) *paṇa* is the stake (*glaha*) in dice; the dice themselves are called *devana* or *pāśaka*. (2.8.1487) *pariṇāya*, however, is the moving of the pieces (*śārī*) all around [the board], and it is not feminine. (2.8.1488) *aṣṭāpada* and *śāriphala* refer to the chessboard; *prāṇivṛtta* and *samāhvaya* refer to gambling with living creatures.

(2.8.1489) Those words which have been stated here as being etymological (*yaugika*) because of their extensive usage in a single [gender], (2.8.1490) those [words] may also occur in another gender when they apply elsewhere by virtue of sharing that same property;
thus ends the section on Śūdras. Herein are 46 root verses. *Kṣe*.
(2.8.1491) Thus, in the *Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana* composed by Amarasimha, the second book (kāṇḍa),
beginning with "the earth" (*bhūmi*), has been fully established along with its supplements.
(2.8.1492) Herein, there are 735 root verses.
(2.8.1493) And all combined: 750; *prakāma* verses 281, *kṣetra* verses 18; all together 299.
(2.8.1494) Likewise, root verses 1017, *kṣetra* verses 32; all together 1049.
